title: Australia | AUSTRAC AML/CTF Compliance (2026 reforms)
tagline: Master Australia's reformed AML/CTF regime: risk assessment, CDD, PEPs, SMRs, tipping off, sanctions and correspondent banking for banks.
sectors: Payments, remittance and correspondent banking teams
Bank compliance, risk and internal audit functions
description:
This quest teaches Australian bank staff the AML/CTF regime as it applies **from 31 March 2026**: the **Anti-Money Laundering and Counter-Terrorism Financing Act 2006** as rebuilt by the **2024 amending Act**, the **AML/CTF Rules 2025**, and the sanctions laws administered by the **Australian Sanctions Office**. It is built around **AUSTRAC**, Australia's AML/CTF regulator and financial intelligence unit.

The reformed Rules require a bank's AML/CTF policies to provide initial and ongoing training, suited to each role, for people who perform AML/CTF functions. This quest is designed for that audience: frontline and branch staff, onboarding and KYC teams, payments and correspondent banking staff, financial crime analysts, managers and directors.

Across five stages you will work through the ML/TF/PF risk assessment and AML/CTF policies, governing body and compliance officer duties, outcome-based CDD, enhanced CDD and PEPs, suspicious matter reports and their deadlines, threshold and international transfer reports, tipping off, record keeping, sanctions screening, correspondent banking and personnel due diligence, following a fictional team at Banksia Harbour Bank in Sydney, Parramatta and Melbourne.

This quest builds knowledge of the law and good practice; it does not replace your institution's own AML/CTF policies, procedures or advice from your compliance team.
audience: Branch, contact centre and frontline staff at Australian banks who provide designated services
Onboarding, KYC and enhanced due diligence teams handling individuals, companies, trusts and PEPs
Payments, international transfers, correspondent banking and sanctions screening staff
Financial crime analysts and investigators who review alerts and prepare SMRs
Managers, senior managers and directors with AML/CTF approval or oversight duties
outcomes: Explain the 2024 reforms, the AML/CTF Rules 2025, the key dates and the roles of AUSTRAC and the Australian Sanctions Office
Describe the ML/TF/PF risk assessment, the AML/CTF policies and the duties of the governing body, senior managers and compliance officer
Apply initial, ongoing and enhanced CDD, including beneficial ownership and PEP rules
Recognise when an SMR is due, meet the 24-hour and 3-business-day deadlines and avoid tipping off
Apply threshold, international transfer and record-keeping requirements
Handle sanctions matches, correspondent banking due diligence and personnel due diligence and training in line with the Act and Rules

quest.name: Harbour Watch
quest.premise: You have just joined the financial crime team at Banksia Harbour Bank in Sydney, months after Australia's AML/CTF reforms went live for banks. With compliance officer Priya Raman, analyst Tom Nguyen, branch manager Jarrah Collins, board risk chair Grace O'Connell and FI banking head Daniel Okafor, you must turn the new rulebook into everyday decisions at the counter, in the payments room and in the boardroom.

badge.name: Harbour Watch Keeper
badge.description: Awarded for demonstrating working knowledge of Australia's reformed AML/CTF and sanctions obligations for banks.

sessions.title: The 2026 reforms, regulators and offences
sessions.summary: Meet the reformed AML/CTF regime: the 2006 Act as rebuilt in 2024, the AML/CTF Rules 2025, the key dates, AUSTRAC and the Australian Sanctions Office, and how AUSTRAC enforces the law.
objectives: Explain how the 2024 amending Act and the AML/CTF Rules 2025 reshaped the AML/CTF Act 2006
Recall the key reform dates for banks, new sectors and the tipping-off offence
Distinguish the roles of AUSTRAC, the Australian Sanctions Office, APRA and ASIC
Describe AUSTRAC's enforcement tools and the lessons of major bank cases

cards.title: Stage one: the new rulebook
cards.setting: Financial crime team, Banksia Harbour Bank head office, Barangaroo, Sydney. 8:50 am.

lines.text: Your access pass works on the second try. On your desk: a laptop, a lanyard and a thick binder labelled 'AML/CTF reforms: what changed on 31 March 2026'.
Morning! I'm Priya Raman, the bank's AML/CTF compliance officer. Welcome to the team that keeps dirty money out of Banksia Harbour.
Tom Nguyen, financial crime analyst. Fair warning: half the bank still talks about the old 'Part A and Part B' program. That world is gone.
(on a video call from the Parramatta branch) Jarrah Collins, branch manager. My tellers keep asking me what actually changed for them. I need answers I can repeat.
Grace O'Connell, chair of the board risk committee. And the board wants to know what the reforms mean for us as directors, not just for the tellers.
So your first mission is the map: which laws apply, who the regulators are, what changed and what happens when a bank gets it wrong.
Five stages, one final exam. By the end, you should be able to explain our AML/CTF obligations to a teller, an analyst and a director. Ready?

scenes.heading: One Act, rebuilt
scenes.narration: Australia's main law is still the Anti-Money Laundering and Counter-Terrorism Financing Act 2006. A 2024 amending Act rebuilt large parts of it, and new AML/CTF Rules made in 2025 replaced the 2007 Rules.

scenes.heading: When it bit
scenes.narration: For banks and other existing reporting entities, most of the new obligations started on 31 March 2026. Newly regulated sectors, such as many lawyers, accountants and real estate agents, followed on 1 July 2026.

scenes.heading: A new program shape
scenes.narration: The old two-part program has gone. A bank now needs a documented ML/TF risk assessment and a set of AML/CTF policies, procedures, systems and controls that manage those risks.

scenes.heading: Three risks, not two
scenes.narration: The risk assessment must now cover proliferation financing as well as money laundering and terrorism financing. That is the funding of weapons of mass destruction programs.

scenes.heading: Outcomes over checklists
scenes.narration: Customer due diligence is now framed as outcomes the bank must establish on reasonable grounds, scaled to the customer's risk, rather than a fixed checklist of identification steps.

scenes.heading: A sharper tipping-off rule
scenes.narration: A redesigned tipping-off offence started a year earlier, on 31 March 2025. It focuses on disclosures that could prejudice an investigation.

cards.title: The reform timeline
cards.caption: Dates from the amending Act and AUSTRAC's reform material. Banks moved on 31 March 2026.

items.label: Amending Act passed
items.detail: Parliament passes the AML/CTF Amendment Act 2024, reshaping programs, CDD and reporting.

items.label: New tipping-off offence
items.detail: The redesigned offence for disclosing suspicious matter information takes effect.

items.label: AML/CTF Rules 2025 made
items.detail: AUSTRAC's new Rules replace the 2007 Rules and fill in the detail of the reformed Act.

items.label: Banks switch over
items.detail: Existing reporting entities, including banks, must meet the new obligations.

items.label: New sectors join
items.detail: Tranche two professions, such as many lawyers, accountants and real estate agents, are regulated.

cards.question: Which body receives suspicious matter reports from Australian banks?
options: The Australian Sanctions Office in DFAT
AUSTRAC, through its CEO
APRA, as prudential supervisor
The Australian Federal Police directly
cards.explanation: Suspicious matter reports go to the AUSTRAC CEO. AUSTRAC is both the AML/CTF regulator and Australia's financial intelligence unit, and it shares intelligence with partner agencies such as the AFP. The ASO handles sanctions, and APRA is the prudential regulator.

cards.title: Who does what
cards.caption: AUSTRAC is the main AML/CTF regulator; sanctions sit with the ASO.

items.label: AUSTRAC
items.left: AML/CTF regulator and financial intelligence unit
items.right: Receives SMRs and other reports, supervises banks, takes enforcement action

items.label: Australian Sanctions Office
items.left: Sits in the Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
items.right: Administers UN and autonomous sanctions, keeps the Consolidated List, issues permits

items.label: APRA
items.left: Prudential regulator of banks
items.right: Looks at governance and risk culture; AML/CTF failures can become prudential concerns

items.label: ASIC
items.left: Conduct and licensing regulator
items.right: Oversees how banks treat customers and run financial services licences

items.label: Law enforcement partners
items.left: Such as the AFP and state police
items.right: Use AUSTRAC intelligence to investigate and prosecute crime

cards.title: Reporting entities and designated services
cards.body:
The Act does not regulate 'banks' as such. It regulates **reporting entities**: businesses that provide **designated services** listed in the Act.

- Opening an account, taking deposits, making loans and sending money are all designated services.
- A bank provides dozens of them, so it is a reporting entity with the full set of obligations.
- Obligations attach to the service: CDD before you **start** providing a designated service, reporting when a designated service involves a suspicious matter or a threshold transaction.

The reformed Act groups those obligations into a few pillars: a **risk assessment**, **AML/CTF policies**, **customer due diligence**, **reporting** to AUSTRAC, **record keeping** and governance duties for the **governing body** and the **AML/CTF compliance officer**. Sanctions duties run alongside, under separate sanctions laws, and the new Rules require the AML/CTF policies to deal with them too.

cards.title: Match the law to its job
cards.prompt: Link each Australian law or instrument to what it does for a bank.

pairs.right: The core statute: risk assessment, policies, CDD, reporting, records and offences
The amending law that rebuilt programs and CDD and added proliferation financing
AUSTRAC's detailed rules, including personnel due diligence and training
Australia's own sanctions regime, with a strict liability offence for companies

pairs.left: Charter of the United Nations Act 1945
pairs.right: Gives effect in Australia to UN Security Council sanctions

cards.title: The board asks the hard question
cards.setting: Board risk committee pre-meeting, level 30, Barangaroo. 4:15 pm.

lines.text: Priya, be blunt. If we get AML/CTF wrong, what actually happens to Banksia Harbour?
AUSTRAC has a toolkit. It can direct us to fix a breach, make us commission an external audit, accept an enforceable undertaking or go to the Federal Court for civil penalty orders.
And the big Australian bank cases were civil penalty proceedings. Commonwealth Bank settled in 2018, Westpac in 2020. Both were about systems that failed at scale.
Systems failing at scale. That's what keeps directors awake.
Which is why the reformed Act gives the governing body its own oversight duty. It's not just a compliance team problem any more.

cards.title: 'The reforms are for lawyers, not us'
cards.situation: At a team meeting, a senior colleague in operations says: 'Relax. The reforms were about bringing lawyers, accountants and real estate agents into the system. Banks were already regulated, so we can keep the old program until the next review cycle.' Several junior staff nod. What do you do?

choices.text: Agree; banks have had AML/CTF programs since 2006, so the reforms are mostly someone else's problem.
choices.outcome: Risky. Banks were regulated before, but the reformed obligations applied to existing reporting entities like Banksia Harbour from 31 March 2026. Keeping the old program design would leave gaps against the new Act.

choices.text: Politely correct it: banks had to meet the reformed obligations from 31 March 2026, and new sectors joined on 1 July 2026. Offer to share Priya's briefing.
choices.outcome: Best. You fix the misunderstanding with the right dates and point people to the official internal briefing. A shared, accurate picture is the start of a working program.

choices.text: Say nothing in the meeting but email the compliance officer later to complain about the colleague.
choices.outcome: Partly right. Telling compliance is sensible, but the team leaves the meeting with a wrong idea. A brief, respectful correction in the moment helps everyone.

cards.title: AUSTRAC's enforcement toolkit
cards.caption: Top = most serious. AUSTRAC chooses the tool that fits the breach; the Federal Court can also grant injunctions.

items.label: Civil penalty orders
items.detail: AUSTRAC applies to the Federal Court; penalties can be very large for systemic failures.

items.label: Enforceable undertakings
items.detail: A binding promise to fix problems, enforceable in court if broken.

items.label: Remedial directions and external audits
items.detail: AUSTRAC can direct a fix, or require an independent audit of compliance.

items.label: Supervision and engagement
items.detail: Compliance assessments, information requests and guidance, day to day.

cards.front: Myth: AUSTRAC is only a regulator.
cards.back: Fact: it is both the AML/CTF regulator and Australia's financial intelligence unit, analysing the reports banks send.

cards.front: Myth: proliferation financing is a sanctions issue only.
cards.back: Fact: since the reforms, the ML/TF risk assessment must also cover proliferation financing risk.

cards.front: Myth: the new tipping-off offence began on 31 March 2026.
cards.back: Fact: it started a year earlier, on 31 March 2025.

cards.front: Myth: a bank's program still has Part A and Part B.
cards.back: Fact: it now has an ML/TF risk assessment plus AML/CTF policies, procedures, systems and controls.

cards.front: Myth: sanctions are handled by AUSTRAC.
cards.back: Fact: the Australian Sanctions Office in DFAT administers sanctions; the AML/CTF policies must still deal with targeted financial sanctions.

cards.question: A colleague asks when the redesigned tipping-off offence took effect. What is the correct answer?
options: 31 March 2025
31 March 2026
1 July 2026
When the 2007 Rules were repealed
cards.explanation: The new tipping-off offence commenced on 31 March 2025, a year before most other changes for banks on 31 March 2026. 1 July 2026 is when newly regulated sectors came in.

cards.title: Real cases: two banks, two lessons
cards.body:
AUSTRAC has taken two of Australia's largest banks to the Federal Court in civil penalty proceedings.

- **Commonwealth Bank (2018).** The case centred on reporting and monitoring failures linked to its intelligent deposit machines, including large numbers of late threshold transaction reports. It ended with a court-approved penalty.
- **Westpac (2020).** The case centred on failures to report international funds transfers and weaknesses in monitoring for risky payment patterns. It also ended with a court-ordered penalty.

**The lessons for you:**
- Small control gaps repeated millions of times become systemic breaches.
- Reporting failures are not just 'paperwork': they deprive AUSTRAC and police of intelligence.
- Boards and senior managers were asked hard questions about oversight, which the reformed Act now makes explicit.

cards.title: Speak the new language
cards.body:
Old habits show up in words. Use the reformed terms:
- **ML/TF risk assessment** (not 'Part A risk section')
- **AML/CTF policies** (the policies, procedures, systems and controls)
- **Governing body** (the board, for a bank)
- **AML/CTF compliance officer**
- **Initial and ongoing CDD**, with **enhanced CDD** where triggered

When staff use the new words, they start thinking in the new structure.

cards.title: Stage one take-aways
items: Australia's AML/CTF regime rests on the AML/CTF Act 2006, rebuilt by the 2024 amending Act, and the AML/CTF Rules 2025.
Banks had to meet the reformed obligations from 31 March 2026; new sectors joined on 1 July 2026; the new tipping-off offence began on 31 March 2025.
AUSTRAC is both regulator and financial intelligence unit; sanctions are administered by the Australian Sanctions Office in DFAT.
A bank's program is now an ML/TF risk assessment plus AML/CTF policies, covering money laundering, terrorism financing and proliferation financing.
AUSTRAC can use remedial directions, external audits, enforceable undertakings and Federal Court civil penalty proceedings.

cards.prompt: Think of your own role. Which designated services do you help provide, and which of the reform changes (risk assessment, outcome-based CDD, PF, governance, tipping off) touches your daily work most?

quiz.question: Which statement best describes how the 2024 reforms changed the structure of a bank's AML/CTF program?
options: It now consists of an ML/TF risk assessment plus AML/CTF policies, procedures, systems and controls
It is now written by AUSTRAC and adopted unchanged by each bank
It keeps the familiar Part A and Part B structure but adds a third part that deals only with proliferation financing risk
It is replaced by a single annual compliance report lodged with AUSTRAC
quiz.explanation: The reformed Act requires an ML/TF risk assessment and AML/CTF policies that manage the risks it identifies. The old Part A/Part B design was replaced, not extended, and each bank must still design its own program.

quiz.question: From what date did existing reporting entities such as banks have to meet most of the reformed AML/CTF obligations?
options: 31 March 2025
10 December 2024
1 July 2026
31 March 2026
quiz.explanation: Most reformed obligations applied to existing reporting entities from 31 March 2026. 31 March 2025 was the start of the new tipping-off offence and 1 July 2026 the start date for newly regulated sectors.

quiz.question: A trade finance manager says proliferation financing is 'just a DFAT sanctions matter' and does not belong in the AML/CTF risk assessment. How should you respond?
options: Disagree, because AUSTRAC now administers the sanctions Consolidated List
Agree, unless the bank finances weapons manufacturers directly
The risk assessment must now cover proliferation financing as well as ML and TF
Agree, because proliferation financing is regulated only under the Autonomous Sanctions Act
quiz.explanation: Since the reforms, the risk assessment must identify and assess money laundering, terrorism financing and proliferation financing risks. Sanctions laws still apply in parallel, but the Consolidated List is kept by the ASO, not AUSTRAC.

quiz.question: Why is a bank a 'reporting entity' under the AML/CTF Act?
options: Because its board chooses to opt in to the AML/CTF regime
Because it lodges suspicious matter reports with AUSTRAC
Because APRA licenses it as an authorised deposit-taking institution under the Banking Act, which brings in AUSTRAC rules
Because it provides designated services listed in the Act, such as accounts, loans and transfers
quiz.explanation: The Act applies to businesses that provide designated services. A bank provides many of them, so it is a reporting entity. Lodging reports is a consequence of being a reporting entity, not the reason it is one.

quiz.question: Banksia Harbour's sanctions screening flags a payment beneficiary as a possible match to the DFAT Consolidated List. Which body administers that list and the sanctions regime behind it?
options: ASIC, through its licensing of financial services
AUSTRAC, as part of its financial intelligence role
The Australian Sanctions Office in the Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
APRA, through its prudential standards on risk
quiz.explanation: The ASO in DFAT administers Australia's UN and autonomous sanctions and keeps the Consolidated List. AUSTRAC is the AML/CTF regulator; the AML/CTF policies must deal with targeted financial sanctions, but the list itself is DFAT's.

quiz.question: AUSTRAC finds that a bank has broken a civil penalty provision but the bank is cooperating. Which response is AUSTRAC able to use without going to court?
options: Give the bank a remedial direction to fix the breach
Order the bank to close all affected accounts
Cancel the bank's banking authority
Impose a criminal conviction on the compliance officer
quiz.explanation: The Act lets the AUSTRAC CEO give remedial directions and accept enforceable undertakings without court proceedings. Banking authorisation is APRA's domain, and criminal convictions require a court.

quiz.question: What do the Commonwealth Bank (2018) and Westpac (2020) AUSTRAC cases most usefully teach frontline and operations staff?
options: Reporting failures matter only if the customer is later convicted
Penalties only arise where staff knowingly help criminals launder money through customer accounts or branches
Only the compliance team is accountable when reports are late
Control gaps repeated across many transactions can become systemic breaches with serious consequences
quiz.explanation: Both cases were civil penalty proceedings about systems and reporting failures at scale, not about staff knowingly laundering money. Missed reports deny intelligence to AUSTRAC and police regardless of any later conviction.

quiz.question: Which instrument contains the detailed requirements on personnel due diligence and AML/CTF training for banks after the reforms?
options: The AML/CTF Rules 2025, together with the Act
APRA's prudential standard on fit and proper
The Banking Code of Practice
The AML/CTF Rules 2007, as amended in 2024
quiz.explanation: The Act requires the AML/CTF policies to deal with personnel due diligence and training, and the AML/CTF Rules 2025 set the detail. The 2007 Rules were replaced, and the other instruments deal with different subjects.

quiz.question: A new graduate says AUSTRAC 'just collects forms'. Which reply is most accurate?
options: It is both the AML/CTF regulator and the financial intelligence unit that analyses reports
AUSTRAC only collects forms; ASIC then analyses them and passes the intelligence on to law enforcement
AUSTRAC is a law enforcement agency that arrests suspects
AUSTRAC only supervises casinos and remitters, not banks
quiz.explanation: AUSTRAC regulates reporting entities and, as the FIU, turns their reports into intelligence for partner agencies. It does not make arrests, and it supervises banks as well as other sectors.

quiz.question: Which pair correctly names the two Australian laws that create sanctions obligations for a bank?
options: The Autonomous Sanctions Act 2011 and the Foreign Acquisitions and Takeovers Act 1975
The Autonomous Sanctions Act 2011 and the Charter of the United Nations Act 1945
The AML/CTF Act 2006 and the Proceeds of Crime Act 2002
The Banking Act 1959 and the Corporations Act 2001
quiz.explanation: UN Security Council sanctions are given effect through the Charter of the United Nations Act 1945, and Australia's own sanctions through the Autonomous Sanctions Act 2011. The AML/CTF Rules require the AML/CTF policies to deal with both.

sessions.title: The AML/CTF program, risk assessment and governing body
sessions.summary: Build the reformed program: the ML/TF/PF risk assessment, the AML/CTF policies, review triggers, and the roles of the governing body, senior managers and the AML/CTF compliance officer.
objectives: Apply the four risk lenses of the ML/TF risk assessment and its review triggers
Explain why a designated service cannot start without an up-to-date risk assessment
Allocate duties between the governing body, designated senior managers and the compliance officer
Describe the compliance officer's standing, functions, AUSTRAC notification and annual board report

cards.title: Stage two: the app that changed the risk
cards.setting: Product committee room, Banksia Harbour Bank, Sydney. Monday, 10:00 am.

lines.text: On the screen: a launch plan for 'Banksia Send', an app feature letting customers pay family in the Pacific and South-East Asia in seconds.
It's a great product. It's also a new service, a new channel and new countries, all at once.
Which means our ML/TF risk assessment has a significant change to deal with before we switch it on.
The business wants to launch in two weeks. Does the board need to be involved?
The board doesn't approve every product, Grace. But the governing body must keep overseeing our risk and compliance, and I report to you at least every twelve months.
So who signs off the updated risk assessment and policies? Not me, I hope.
Senior managers designated in our policies. Stage two is about exactly that: the risk engine, the policies, and who owns what.

scenes.heading: Start with your own risks
scenes.narration: Every bank must carry out an ML/TF risk assessment that identifies and assesses the money laundering, terrorism financing and proliferation financing risks it may reasonably face in providing its services.

scenes.heading: Four lenses
scenes.narration: For services provided in Australia, the assessment must consider the kinds of services, the kinds of customers, the delivery channels including new technologies, and the countries the bank deals with.

scenes.heading: Keep it current
scenes.narration: The assessment must be reviewed when something significant changes, when AUSTRAC shares relevant risk information, and in any event at least once every three years.

scenes.heading: No assessment, no service
scenes.narration: A bank must not start providing a designated service if its risk assessment is not up to date for that service. Each service provided while out of date can be a separate contravention.

scenes.heading: Policies that match
scenes.narration: The AML/CTF policies, procedures, systems and controls must manage the risks the assessment finds, ensure compliance with the law, and suit the bank's nature, size and complexity.

cards.title: The AML/CTF program cycle
cards.caption: A loop, not a one-off document: each review feeds the next assessment.

items.label: Assess ML/TF/PF risk
items.detail: Services, customers, channels and countries

items.label: Design policies and controls
items.detail: Proportionate to the risks and to the bank's size and complexity

items.label: Approve
items.detail: Designated senior managers approve the risk assessment and policies

items.label: Apply and monitor
items.detail: Staff follow the policies; the compliance officer oversees day to day

items.label: Inform the governing body
items.detail: Compliance officer reports at least every 12 months

items.label: Review and update
items.detail: On significant change, AUSTRAC input, and at least every 3 years

cards.question: At a minimum, how often must a bank review its ML/TF risk assessment even if nothing significant changes?
options: Every 12 months
At least once every 3 years
Only when AUSTRAC asks
Every 7 years
cards.explanation: The Act sets a backstop of at least once every three years, on top of event-driven reviews when there is a significant change or AUSTRAC communicates relevant risk information. The 12-month figure is the compliance officer's reporting cycle to the governing body.

cards.title: Who owns what
cards.caption: Each layer has its own legal role under the reformed Act and Rules.

items.label: Governing body
items.detail: The board: ongoing oversight of risk and compliance; takes reasonable steps to ensure the bank manages risk.

items.label: Designated senior managers
items.detail: Approve the ML/TF risk assessment and the AML/CTF policies.

items.label: AML/CTF compliance officer
items.detail: Management level; oversees day-to-day compliance and talks to AUSTRAC.

items.label: Business lines and personnel
items.detail: Apply the policies in every account, payment and review.

cards.title: Whose duty is it?
cards.prompt: Sort each duty to the role the reformed Act or Rules give it.

items.text: Exercise ongoing oversight of the bank's risk identification and compliance
Take reasonable steps to ensure the bank manages its ML/TF/PF risks
Approve the ML/TF risk assessment
Approve the AML/CTF policies
Oversee and coordinate day-to-day compliance with the Act and Rules
Communicate with AUSTRAC on the bank's behalf
Report on compliance and risk management at least every 12 months

cards.title: The AML/CTF compliance officer
cards.body:
Every reporting entity must designate an individual as its **AML/CTF compliance officer**. For a bank, the reformed Act and Rules expect a lot from that role:

- **Management level**, with enough **authority, independence and resources** to do the job.
- Functions include overseeing **day-to-day compliance** with the Act and Rules, overseeing the operation of the **AML/CTF policies** and **communicating with AUSTRAC**.
- The bank must **notify AUSTRAC** who its compliance officer is within **14 days** of designating them.
- The policies must provide for the compliance officer to **report to the governing body** on compliance and risk management **at least once every 12 months**.

A compliance officer buried three levels below the business, without budget or a line to the board, does not meet the spirit or the letter of the reforms.

lines.text: Priya, the product owner says Banksia Send goes live Monday. The risk assessment update is still a draft and no senior manager has approved the new controls.
Then it can't go live Monday. Starting a designated service without an up-to-date risk assessment is a contravention in its own right.
(on the phone) I've had the business on to me, Priya. They say it's only a few weeks' delay in the assessment.
Grace, the board's job is oversight. I'll give you the facts tonight: what's missing, what it would take and the new date.

cards.title: Launch now, assess later?
cards.situation: The product owner proposes launching Banksia Send on Monday with ordinary transaction monitoring, and finishing the updated risk assessment and policy changes 'within the quarter'. The new feature introduces new corridors to Pacific and South-East Asian countries and a new instant channel. You are asked for compliance's view.

choices.text: Support the launch: the existing monitoring will catch anything serious, and the paperwork can follow.
choices.outcome: Poor. The Act prohibits starting a designated service if the risk assessment is not up to date for it, and each service provided can be a separate contravention. Monitoring alone does not cure that.

choices.text: Advise delaying launch until the risk assessment is updated for the new services, channel and countries, controls are adjusted and designated senior managers approve.
choices.outcome: Best. You tie the advice to the legal requirement, cover all four risk lenses and route approval to the right people. The governing body is informed through the compliance officer.

choices.text: Allow a soft launch to staff and friends-and-family customers only, while the assessment is finished.
choices.outcome: Partly right. Limiting exposure is sensible, but if the service is provided to customers at all, it still needs an up-to-date risk assessment first.

cards.title: Old program versus reformed program
cards.caption: The reformed design ties every control back to an assessed risk.

items.label: Shape
items.left: Part A (general) and Part B (customer identification)
items.right: ML/TF risk assessment plus AML/CTF policies

items.label: Risks covered
items.left: Money laundering and terrorism financing
items.right: ML, TF and proliferation financing

items.label: Approval
items.left: Board and senior management oversight
items.right: Named senior managers approve; governing body has a statutory oversight duty

items.label: Review
items.left: Kept up to date
items.right: Event-driven reviews plus a 3-year backstop for both assessment and policies

items.label: Training
items.left: Risk awareness training program
items.right: Personnel due diligence and role-based training inside the policies

cards.title: Updating the program for a new product
cards.prompt: Put the steps in a sensible order for bringing a new product into the AML/CTF program.
steps: Identify the significant change: new service, channel, customers or countries
Assess the ML/TF/PF risks the change brings
Adjust the AML/CTF policies, procedures, systems and controls
Designated senior managers approve the updated assessment and policies
Train affected staff and switch on monitoring before launch
Report the change and its risks to the governing body through the compliance officer

cards.back: The individual or group with primary responsibility for governance and oversight; for a bank, its board.
The bank's documented assessment of the ML, TF and PF risks it may reasonably face in providing its services.
The policies, procedures, systems and controls that manage those risks and ensure compliance.
A senior manager named in the policies as responsible for approving the risk assessment and policies.
Controls must suit the nature, size and complexity of the business.

cards.question: Banksia Harbour designates a new AML/CTF compliance officer on 2 June. What must the bank do?
options: Nothing, unless AUSTRAC asks
Notify AUSTRAC within 14 days of the designation
Get APRA's approval before the appointment
Publish the name in its annual report
cards.explanation: The Act requires a reporting entity to notify AUSTRAC of its designated compliance officer within 14 days. APRA approval and publication are not AML/CTF Act requirements.

cards.title: Inside Banksia Harbour's board paper
cards.body:
Priya's annual report to the board risk committee (a fictional example) is short and specific:

- **Risk picture:** the updated risk assessment rates Banksia Send corridors as higher risk because of speed, new countries and limited payee information.
- **Controls:** a new payee-screening step, lower first-month limits and a monitoring scenario for rapid fan-out payments.
- **Compliance:** two late international transfer reports caused by a file error, fixed and reviewed; no SMR deadline breaches.
- **People:** completion rates for role-based AML/CTF training, by team, with overdue staff named to their managers.
- **Asks:** budget for a second sanctions analyst.

Grace's committee challenges the monitoring scenario and asks for a follow-up in six months. That challenge and follow-up is what ongoing oversight looks like in practice.

cards.title: Stage two take-aways
items: The ML/TF risk assessment covers ML, TF and PF risk through four lenses: services, customers, channels and countries.
Review it on significant change, on AUSTRAC risk information, and at least every 3 years; the policies also need a review at least every 3 years.
A bank must not start a designated service without an up-to-date risk assessment for it.
The governing body oversees; designated senior managers approve; the compliance officer runs day-to-day compliance and reports at least every 12 months.
The compliance officer must be at management level with authority, independence and resources, and AUSTRAC must be told who it is within 14 days.

cards.prompt: Which product, channel or customer group in your area changed in the last year? Was the risk assessment updated before the change went live, and who approved it?

quiz.question: Which four matters must a bank providing services in Australia have regard to in its ML/TF risk assessment?
options: Its customers, complaints, products and branch locations
Its staff, premises, suppliers and auditors
Its services, customers, delivery channels and the countries it deals with
Its capital, liquidity, earnings and market share
quiz.explanation: The Act directs the assessment to the kinds of services, kinds of customers, delivery channels (including new technologies) and countries. The other lists mix prudential or operational factors that are not the statutory lenses.

quiz.question: Banksia Harbour plans to start offering accounts to a new class of non-resident customers through a fully digital channel. What must happen before it starts providing the service?
options: The board must approve the product terms
AUSTRAC must approve the new product in writing
The ML/TF risk assessment must be reviewed and up to date for the new service
The compliance officer must lodge a notice with APRA
quiz.explanation: A significant change to customers or channels triggers a review, and the bank must not start the service if the assessment is out of date. AUSTRAC does not pre-approve products, and the board's role is oversight rather than product approval.

quiz.question: Who must approve a bank's ML/TF risk assessment and AML/CTF policies under the reformed Act?
options: AUSTRAC's supervision team
The bank's external auditor
One or more senior managers designated in the AML/CTF policies
The AML/CTF compliance officer acting alone
quiz.explanation: The policies must designate senior managers responsible for approving both the risk assessment and the policies. The compliance officer oversees compliance but is not the statutory approver, and AUSTRAC does not approve programs.

quiz.question: What is the governing body's own duty under the reformed Act?
options: Ongoing oversight of risk and compliance, and reasonable steps to ensure risks are managed
To act as the AML/CTF compliance officer whenever that role is vacant or the officer is on leave
To approve each new high-risk customer personally
To review every suspicious matter report before it is lodged
quiz.explanation: The governing body must oversee the risk assessment process and compliance, and take reasonable steps to ensure risks are managed. It is not expected to review SMRs or approve individual customers.

quiz.question: How often must the AML/CTF policies provide for the compliance officer to report to the governing body?
options: At least once every 12 months
Only after a significant breach
Every quarter
At least once every 3 years
quiz.explanation: The Rules require the policies to provide for compliance officer reporting to the governing body at least every 12 months. Three years is the backstop for reviewing the risk assessment and policies.

quiz.question: A small Banksia Harbour subsidiary copies the parent bank's 400-page policies word for word, although it offers only two simple products. Which requirement is most at risk?
options: Policies must be approved by AUSTRAC before use
Policies must be identical across a corporate group
Policies must be appropriate to the nature, size and complexity of the business
Policies must be reviewed every 12 months
quiz.explanation: The Act requires AML/CTF policies to suit the entity's nature, size and complexity and to manage its own assessed risks. There is no AUSTRAC pre-approval, no rule that group policies must be identical, and the policy review backstop is three years.

quiz.question: AUSTRAC publishes a risk assessment highlighting a new laundering method through instant payment apps, which Banksia Harbour offers. What does the Act expect?
options: Report the AUSTRAC publication to the governing body only, and leave the risk assessment as it is until the next review
Wait for the next three-yearly review
Lodge an SMR on all instant-payment customers
Review the bank's ML/TF risk assessment, because AUSTRAC has communicated relevant risk information
quiz.explanation: When AUSTRAC communicates information that identifies or assesses risks relevant to the bank's services, a review is triggered. Waiting for the backstop ignores the trigger, and blanket SMRs without suspicion are inappropriate.

quiz.question: Which description best fits the reformed position of the AML/CTF compliance officer?
options: A management-level individual with sufficient authority, independence and resources
Any employee who has completed AML/CTF training
An external consultant engaged for the annual review
A board director who chairs the risk committee
quiz.explanation: The Act requires the compliance officer to be at management level with enough authority, independence and resources. The role is distinct from the governing body and is not filled simply by training completion.

quiz.question: Banksia Harbour launched a new service without updating its risk assessment and provided it to 300 customers over ten days. How does the Act treat this?
options: There is no breach if no suspicious activity occurred
Each service provided while the assessment was out of date can be a separate contravention
It is treated as one single breach, however many customers received the service during those ten days
It is a breach only if AUSTRAC warned the bank first
quiz.explanation: The Act provides that a separate contravention occurs for each designated service provided, and on each day, while the requirement is not met. The breach does not depend on suspicious activity or a prior warning.

quiz.question: Which change is the clearest example of the 'significant change' that should trigger a review of the risk assessment?
options: Replacing the colour scheme of the internet banking site
Moving a branch to a new address in the same suburb
Renaming a savings account and refreshing its brochure without changing any features
Launching payments to several new countries through a new mobile channel
quiz.explanation: New countries and new delivery channels are two of the four lenses the risk assessment must consider, so this change is significant. Cosmetic or minor location changes do not alter the ML/TF/PF risk profile.

sessions.title: Customer due diligence, enhanced CDD and PEPs
sessions.summary: Work through outcome-based initial CDD, ongoing CDD, the section 32 enhanced CDD triggers and the rules for domestic, foreign and international organisation PEPs.
objectives: List the matters initial CDD must establish on reasonable grounds before a service starts
Apply ongoing CDD when a customer's behaviour changes
Identify the section 32 triggers for mandatory enhanced CDD
Handle foreign, domestic and international organisation PEPs, including senior manager approval

cards.title: Stage three: the customer at the gate
cards.setting: Business banking desk, Banksia Harbour Bank, Parramatta branch. 11:20 am.

lines.text: A well-dressed visitor wants to open a business account for 'Coral Bay Holdings Pty Ltd', a new import company.
Priya, quick one. The director is pleasant, the ID is fine, but the company's shares are held by a trust, and the trust's beneficiary is a Fijian-registered company.
So who actually owns and controls Coral Bay? Until we've established that on reasonable grounds, we don't start providing the service.
There's more. The director mentioned his uncle is a sitting minister in another country's government, and the uncle 'helps with introductions'.
If the uncle is a beneficial owner or acts for the company, that's a foreign PEP, and enhanced CDD is mandatory.
Stage three, everyone: initial CDD, ongoing CDD, enhanced CDD and PEPs. Let's open Coral Bay's file properly.

cards.title: Initial CDD: what you must establish

scenes.heading: Who is the customer?
scenes.narration: Before starting a designated service, the bank must establish on reasonable grounds who the customer is. For an individual, that means reasonable steps to confirm they are who they claim to be.

scenes.heading: Who else is involved?
scenes.narration: It must also establish who the customer is acting for, who is acting on the customer's behalf and their authority, and, for a company or trust, the beneficial owners.

scenes.heading: PEP or sanctioned?
scenes.narration: The bank must establish whether the customer, a beneficial owner, or anyone acting for or on behalf of the customer is a politically exposed person or a person designated for targeted financial sanctions.

scenes.heading: Why are they here?
scenes.narration: It must understand the nature and purpose of the business relationship or occasional transaction.

scenes.heading: Scaled to risk
scenes.narration: The bank rates the customer's ML/TF risk, collects KYC information appropriate to that risk, and verifies it using reliable and independent data, more for higher risk.

cards.title: The initial CDD path
cards.caption: Outcome-based: the Act sets what must be established, the bank's policies set how.

items.label: Collect KYC information
items.detail: Identity, ownership, agents, purpose; more for higher risk

items.label: Identify the customer's ML/TF risk
items.detail: Based on KYC information reasonably available before service starts

items.label: Verify with reliable, independent data
items.detail: Documents or electronic sources, scaled to the risk

items.label: Screen for PEP and sanctions status
items.detail: Customer, beneficial owners, agents and anyone the customer acts for

items.label: Decide: standard or enhanced CDD
items.detail: Apply enhanced measures where a trigger applies

items.label: Start the service or decline
items.detail: Only once each matter is established on reasonable grounds

cards.question: Under the reformed Act, when must initial CDD be completed for a new customer?
options: Within 10 business days of opening the account
Before the bank starts providing the designated service, subject to limited exceptions
Only if the customer deposits AUD 10,000 or more
Within the first 12 months of the relationship
cards.explanation: The bank must not start providing a designated service until it has established the required matters on reasonable grounds, apart from exceptions the Act and Rules allow. Ten business days is a reporting deadline, and AUD 10,000 is the threshold transaction figure, not a CDD trigger.

cards.title: Enhanced CDD triggers
cards.prompt: Match each trigger in section 32 of the Act to an example at Banksia Harbour.

pairs.right: A cash-intensive business with complex offshore ownership rated high risk
The bank formed a suspicion, lodged an SMR and decides to keep the account open
The beneficial owner is a serving minister in another country
A company formed in a country FATF has called on members to apply enhanced due diligence to
An overseas remitter uses the bank's services to serve its own customers abroad

cards.title: Politically exposed persons in Australia
cards.body:
The Act recognises three kinds of **politically exposed person (PEP)**:

- **Domestic PEPs:** people holding prominent public positions in Australia.
- **Foreign PEPs:** people holding prominent positions in or for a foreign government, such as heads of state, ministers, senior judges, ambassadors, senior military officers, and heads or board members of state-owned companies.
- **International organisation PEPs:** senior people in bodies such as UN agencies.

**What the bank must do:**
- Establish, during CDD, whether the customer, a beneficial owner, anyone the customer acts for, or anyone acting for the customer is a PEP.
- **Foreign PEP:** enhanced CDD is always required, and the Rules require **senior manager approval** before serving them.
- **Domestic or international organisation PEP:** enhanced CDD and senior manager approval where the ML/TF risk is high.

Being a PEP is not an accusation. It is a risk position that needs more care.

cards.title: A familiar customer, a new pattern
cards.setting: Transaction monitoring hub, Barangaroo. Two months later, 3:05 pm.

lines.text: Remember Bilby Logistics? Low-risk freight customer for six years. This month, round-sum transfers in from twelve unrelated people, then straight out to a crypto exchange.
That's ongoing CDD in action. The Act expects us to monitor for unusual transactions and behaviours and to review the customer's risk when they appear.
The owner told my team they've 'diversified into consulting'. Nothing on file supports it.
Then we review and update Bilby's risk rating, refresh the KYC information and decide whether an SMR is due. A six-year history doesn't freeze the risk rating.

cards.title: The minister's nephew
cards.situation: Coral Bay Holdings' file shows the director's uncle, a serving foreign minister, holds 40% of the trust's beneficiary company. The relationship manager says: 'He's a big introducer and the account is only for imports. Can we treat it as a normal small-business account and tidy up the PEP paperwork later?'

choices.text: Agree; the account purpose is ordinary trade, so standard CDD is proportionate.
choices.outcome: Poor. A foreign PEP who is a beneficial owner triggers enhanced CDD under section 32 whatever the account purpose, and the Rules require senior manager approval before the bank serves them.

choices.text: Apply enhanced CDD: establish source of wealth and funds, understand the ownership chain, and obtain senior manager approval before opening.
choices.outcome: Best. You apply the mandatory trigger, look deeper at where the money comes from and route approval to a senior manager as the Rules require. The account may still open if the risk is acceptable.

choices.text: Decline the customer immediately; PEP accounts are not allowed.
choices.outcome: Partly right on caution, but wrong on the law. PEPs are not banned; they need enhanced CDD and senior approval. Blanket refusal can also be unfair to legitimate customers.

cards.title: Initial versus ongoing CDD
cards.caption: Both feed the same customer risk picture.

items.label: When
items.left: Before the bank starts providing the designated service
items.right: Throughout the business relationship

items.label: Core task
items.left: Establish identity, ownership, agents, PEP and sanctions status, and purpose
items.right: Monitor for unusual transactions and behaviours

items.label: Risk rating
items.left: Set from KYC information available at the start
items.right: Reviewed and updated when things change or look unusual

items.label: Information
items.left: Collected and verified in line with risk
items.right: Kept up to date, refreshed when needed

items.label: Output
items.left: Decision to provide the service, with standard or enhanced measures
items.right: Updated rating, enhanced measures, possible SMR or exit

cards.title: Enhanced or standard?
cards.prompt: Sort each customer at Banksia Harbour: does a section 32 trigger make enhanced CDD mandatory, or can the bank apply standard, risk-based CDD?

items.text: A beneficial owner is a foreign ambassador
The customer is rated high ML/TF risk
An SMR has been lodged and the bank keeps serving the customer
A company formed in a jurisdiction on FATF's call-for-action list
An overseas bank customer in a nested services relationship
A local café owner with a modest, steady turnover
A retiree opening a term deposit with pension funds
A domestic PEP assessed as low risk

cards.back: The individual who ultimately owns or controls a company, trust or other customer, directly or indirectly.
Verification sources the customer does not control, such as government records or trusted electronic databases.
An agent, signatory or representative; the bank must establish who they are and their authority.
Where an overseas financial institution, remitter or virtual asset provider uses the bank's services to serve its own customers abroad, outside a correspondent relationship.
The standard the bank must meet: an objective basis, not a hunch or a box ticked.
Information about the customer used to identify them and assess their ML/TF risk.

cards.question: Tom's alert shows a long-standing low-risk customer suddenly receiving funds from many unrelated people. What does ongoing CDD require first?
options: Close the account immediately
Review and, where appropriate, update the customer's risk assessment and KYC information
Wait for the scheduled annual review
Tell the customer the account is under investigation
cards.explanation: Unusual transactions and behaviours that may give rise to an SMR are a specific trigger to review and update the customer's ML/TF risk. Closing the account or telling the customer are not the first step, and telling them could tip them off.

cards.title: Coral Bay Holdings: the file
cards.body:
In this fictional case, Banksia Harbour's enhanced CDD on Coral Bay Holdings went like this:

- **Ownership:** the team mapped the chain from Coral Bay to the trust, to the Fijian company and to three individuals, including the minister uncle at 40%.
- **Verification:** company and trust records from official registers; identity verified electronically for each beneficial owner.
- **Source of wealth and funds:** declared business income, checked against public information on the uncle's role and assets.
- **Approval:** the file went to a designated senior manager, who approved with conditions: lower limits, quarterly reviews and monitoring of payments to the uncle's home country.

Six months later, monitoring caught payments to a consultancy linked to a government tender. The team reviewed the relationship and lodged an SMR.

cards.title: Don't open first and ask later
cards.body: The most common CDD mistake is commercial pressure: 'open it now, we'll chase the documents'. Under the reformed Act the starting point is the reverse: **establish the required matters first**, then start the service, using only the exceptions your bank's policies allow. If you can't establish ownership or purpose, escalate. Don't improvise.

cards.title: Stage three take-aways
items: Initial CDD: establish identity, who the customer acts for, agents and their authority, beneficial owners, PEP and sanctions status, and purpose, before the service starts.
Collect and verify KYC information with reliable, independent data, scaled to the customer's ML/TF risk.
Ongoing CDD means monitoring for unusual activity and reviewing the customer's risk when things change.
Enhanced CDD is mandatory for high risk, continued service after an SMR, foreign PEPs, FATF high-risk jurisdiction links and nested services relationships.
Foreign PEPs always need enhanced CDD and senior manager approval; domestic and international organisation PEPs need them where the risk is high.

cards.prompt: Think of a customer file you handled recently. Could you show, on reasonable grounds, who really owns and controls the customer and why they want the service?

quiz.question: A new customer wants an account today, but the bank has not yet identified the beneficial owners of the company. What does the reformed Act require?
options: Open the account now and identify the beneficial owners at any point within the first 12 months
Open the account if the director's identity is verified
Open the account and lodge a threshold transaction report
The bank must not start the service until the owners are established, subject to exceptions
quiz.explanation: Section 28 prohibits starting a designated service before the required matters, including beneficial owners, are established on reasonable grounds, subject to exceptions in the Act and Rules. Verifying only the director is not enough.

quiz.question: Which of these is NOT one of the matters a bank must establish during initial CDD?
options: Whether a beneficial owner is a politically exposed person
Whether the customer is designated for targeted financial sanctions
The customer's credit score and ability to repay
The nature and purpose of the business relationship
quiz.explanation: Initial CDD covers identity, persons acting for or on behalf of the customer, beneficial owners, PEP and sanctions status, and purpose. Creditworthiness is a lending question, not an AML/CTF CDD matter.

quiz.question: A beneficial owner of a new corporate customer is a serving ambassador of another country. What follows?
options: The bank must refuse the customer
Enhanced CDD is mandatory and a senior manager must approve the relationship
Standard CDD applies unless the account is rated high risk
The bank must lodge an SMR before opening the account
quiz.explanation: A foreign PEP who is a beneficial owner triggers enhanced CDD under section 32, and the Rules require senior manager approval. PEPs are not banned, and being a PEP is not, on its own, grounds for suspicion.

quiz.question: Banksia Harbour lodged an SMR on a customer last week and decides to keep the account open. What does the Act require?
options: Close the account within 3 business days
Tell the customer that a report has been lodged
Nothing further until AUSTRAC responds
Apply enhanced CDD measures appropriate to the customer's risk
quiz.explanation: Where an SMR obligation has arisen and the bank proposes to continue providing services, section 32 makes enhanced CDD mandatory. There is no automatic closure duty, and telling the customer could be tipping off.

quiz.question: A domestic PEP, a local councillor with a small salary account, is assessed as low risk. What is the correct approach?
options: Treat the councillor as a foreign PEP
Always apply enhanced CDD to any PEP
Refuse service, because any PEP relationship creates reputational risk that the bank cannot manage
Apply risk-based CDD; enhanced CDD and senior approval are needed only if the risk is high
quiz.explanation: For domestic and international organisation PEPs, enhanced CDD and senior manager approval apply where the ML/TF risk is high. Only foreign PEPs trigger enhanced CDD automatically.

quiz.question: What does ongoing CDD require when a long-standing customer starts behaving unusually in a way that may give rise to an SMR?
options: Restart initial CDD from the beginning
Ask the customer to explain the activity in writing before doing anything else at all
Review and, where appropriate, update the customer's ML/TF risk assessment
Wait until the next scheduled periodic review
quiz.explanation: Section 30 lists unusual transactions and behaviours that may give rise to an SMR as a trigger to review and update the customer's risk. Waiting ignores the trigger, and questioning the customer carelessly could tip them off.

quiz.question: Which verification approach best meets the reformed CDD standard for a higher-risk customer?
options: Verifying only the information the customer volunteers
Verifying more of the KYC information using reliable and independent data sources
Accepting the customer's own spreadsheet of ownership
Relying only on a reference letter from the customer's long-standing external accountant
quiz.explanation: The Act requires verification with reliable and independent data, in proportion to risk, so a higher-risk customer needs more verification. Customer-prepared documents or a single reference are not independent.

quiz.question: An overseas remittance company asks Banksia Harbour for an account that it will use to send its own customers' payments abroad. There is no correspondent banking relationship. How should this be treated?
options: As an ordinary business account with standard CDD
As a nested services relationship, which requires enhanced CDD
As a threshold transaction that must be reported
As a correspondent banking relationship needing a vostro assessment
quiz.explanation: A nested services relationship is one where a remitter, VASP or financial institution uses the bank's services to serve its own customers in another country, outside correspondent banking. Section 32 makes enhanced CDD mandatory.

quiz.question: During CDD, a customer appoints her financial adviser to operate the account. What must the bank establish about the adviser?
options: The adviser's identity and their authority to act for the customer
Nothing, because only the customer is the bank's customer
The adviser's own source of wealth
Only the adviser's professional licence number
quiz.explanation: The Act requires the bank to establish the identity of any person acting on behalf of the customer and their authority to act. A licence number alone does not do that, and source of wealth is not the standard requirement for an agent.

quiz.question: Which situation triggers enhanced CDD because of a link to a FATF high-risk jurisdiction?
options: The customer holds a foreign passport from any non-FATF member
The customer is a company formed in a jurisdiction for which FATF has called for enhanced due diligence
The customer once visited a country on FATF's increased monitoring list during a family holiday some years ago
The customer's payments are made in a foreign currency
quiz.explanation: Section 32 covers individuals physically present in, and bodies formed in, a high-risk jurisdiction for which FATF has called for enhanced due diligence. A past visit, nationality or foreign currency are not the statutory trigger.

sessions.title: Suspicious matter reports, tipping off and records
sessions.summary: Know when an SMR obligation arises and its 24-hour and 3-business-day deadlines, the threshold and international transfer reports, the tipping-off offence and the 7-year record rules.
objectives: Recognise when an SMR obligation arises and apply the correct deadline
Distinguish SMRs from threshold transaction and international value transfer reports
Avoid tipping off when customers or third parties ask questions
Apply the record retention periods for transaction and CDD records

cards.title: Stage four: the signal in the noise
cards.setting: Financial crime hub, Barangaroo, Sydney. Tuesday, 9:40 am.

lines.text: Tom's screen shows a cluster: nine cash deposits of between AUD 9,000 and AUD 9,900 into one account, across four branches, in three days.
Each deposit is just under the AUD 10,000 threshold. Different branches, same account. That's not a coincidence.
Two of those deposits were at Parramatta. My teller remembers the depositor asking what the 'reporting limit' was.
And there's a second alert: small transfers from several customers to an overseas 'charity' with no registration we can find, in a region with known terrorist activity.
If we suspect terrorism financing, the clock is 24 hours, not 3 business days.
Exactly. Stage four is the signal room: suspicious matter reports, the other reports we owe AUSTRAC, tipping off and the records that prove it all.

scenes.heading: A service moment
scenes.narration: The obligation can arise when the bank starts or proposes to provide a designated service, when a person asks for one, or even when a person just asks whether the bank would provide one.

scenes.heading: A suspicion on reasonable grounds
scenes.narration: It then needs a suspicion on reasonable grounds, for example that the person is not who they claim to be, or that information may be relevant to tax evasion, a crime, proceeds of crime or terrorism financing.

scenes.heading: Two clocks
scenes.narration: If the suspicion relates to terrorism financing, the report is due within 24 hours of forming it. For most other suspicions, within 3 business days.

scenes.heading: To AUSTRAC
scenes.narration: The report goes to the AUSTRAC CEO. The bank keeps serving or exits according to its policies, and applies enhanced CDD if the relationship continues.

scenes.heading: Then silence
scenes.narration: Information that a report has been made, or is required, must not be disclosed in a way that could prejudice an investigation.

cards.title: Numbers every banker should know
cards.caption: All from the AML/CTF Act as amended. Check your bank's procedures for internal deadlines, which are often tighter.

items.label: SMR: terrorism financing
items.detail: From forming the suspicion

items.label: SMR: other suspicions
items.detail: After the day the suspicion is formed

items.label: Threshold transaction
items.detail: Physical currency at or above this amount

items.label: TTR and transfer reports
items.detail: Deadline for threshold and international value transfer reports

items.label: Record retention
items.detail: Transaction records from creation; CDD records after the relationship ends

cards.question: Banksia Harbour's analyst forms a suspicion at 2 pm Wednesday that a customer is sending funds to finance terrorism. By when must the SMR reach AUSTRAC?
options: Within 24 hours of forming the suspicion
Within 3 business days
Within 10 business days
By the end of the month
cards.explanation: For suspected terrorism financing, section 41 requires the SMR within 24 hours after the suspicion is formed. Three business days applies to most other suspicions, and ten business days is the deadline for threshold and transfer reports.

cards.title: The other reports banks owe AUSTRAC
cards.body:
SMRs are triggered by suspicion. Two other regular reports are triggered by **facts**, with no suspicion needed:

- **Threshold transaction reports (TTRs):** when a designated service involves a transfer of **physical currency of AUD 10,000 or more**, the bank must report it within **10 business days** after the transaction.
- **International value transfer reports:** when the bank sends or receives an international transfer of value through its Australian operations, it must report within **10 business days** after passing on or receiving the transfer message. Many staff still call these IFTIs.

**Watch out for structuring.** Customers who split cash into amounts just under AUD 10,000, or ask about the 'reporting limit', are a classic red flag. A TTR is not required for each small deposit, but the pattern may well need an SMR.

cards.title: Which report?
cards.prompt: Sort each situation into the report it most clearly triggers.

items.text: A customer deposits AUD 15,000 in cash for a car purchase, with documents that check out
A customer splits AUD 38,000 in cash into deposits just under AUD 10,000 across branches
A business sends USD 50,000 from Sydney to a supplier in Vietnam
An applicant's passport photo does not match the person in front of you
A customer withdraws AUD 12,000 in cash from their own account
Banksia Harbour receives an incoming transfer from a bank in Singapore for a customer
Small transfers from many customers to an unregistered overseas charity in a conflict zone

cards.title: The phone call
cards.setting: Parramatta branch, back office. Wednesday, 10:15 am.

lines.text: The customer from the cash deposits just rang. He's angry his transfer is 'stuck' and asked if we've 'reported him to the government'.
My newest teller nearly said, 'Compliance is looking at your account because of the cash.' I stopped her mid-sentence.
Good catch, Jarrah. Telling him we're reviewing or reporting could prejudice an investigation. That's what the tipping-off offence is about.
So what do we say? We can't just hang up on him.
Ordinary, true service language: the payment is being processed under our usual checks, and we'll contact him when it's done. No hints, no lies, no speculation.

cards.title: 'Have you reported me?'
cards.situation: A customer whose account is the subject of an SMR lodged yesterday visits the branch. He demands to know why a large transfer was delayed and asks directly: 'Has the bank reported me to AUSTRAC?' You are at the counter.

choices.text: Reassure him: 'Don't worry, we only report people the police are already investigating.'
choices.outcome: Poor. It is false, it hints at the reporting process and it could still prejudice an investigation. Never comment on whether a report exists.

choices.text: Use neutral service language: the transaction is going through the bank's standard checks and he will be contacted; then escalate the interaction to compliance.
choices.outcome: Best. You do not confirm or deny any report, you give an honest, ordinary answer and you tell compliance about the contact, which may itself be useful information.

choices.text: Tell him you are not allowed to discuss whether a report was lodged, because the law forbids it.
choices.outcome: Partly right. You avoided confirming it, but saying the law forbids discussing a report strongly signals one exists. Neutral service language is safer.

cards.title: Tipping off: what the offence covers

cards.back: The bank and its officers, employees and agents, among others, including former staff.
That an SMR has been or must be given, the report or a copy, information from it such as the suspicion, and certain AUSTRAC notices.
When the disclosure would or could reasonably be expected to prejudice an investigation.
No. The Act says it does not matter whether an investigation has begun.
A criminal offence carrying up to 2 years' imprisonment, a fine, or both.
Yes. Disclosures to AUSTRAC entrusted persons are outside the offence, and other exceptions exist in the Act.

cards.title: From red flag to report
cards.prompt: Put the steps a frontline officer and the bank should follow in order.
steps: Notice the unusual activity or behaviour
Record the facts objectively, without alerting the customer
Escalate through the bank's internal unusual-activity channel
Investigator reviews the customer, history and related accounts
Bank decides whether a suspicion is formed on reasonable grounds
Lodge the SMR with AUSTRAC within 24 hours (TF) or 3 business days
Apply enhanced CDD if the relationship continues and keep the records

cards.title: Records and how long to keep them
cards.caption: From Part 10 of the Act. Your bank's policies may require more.

items.label: Transaction records
items.left: Enough to reconstruct each transaction
items.right: 7 years from the day the record is made

items.label: CDD records
items.left: Records showing how the bank met its CDD obligations
items.right: 7 years after the relationship ends or the occasional transaction completes

items.label: Correspondent banking records
items.left: Due diligence assessments and related records
items.right: 7 years after the record is prepared

items.label: Language
items.left: Records must be in English or readily convertible
items.right: Applies to CDD records

cards.question: A customer relationship ended on 1 May 2026. Until when must Banksia Harbour keep the records showing how it met its CDD obligations?
options: Until 1 May 2033
Until 1 May 2031
For 7 years from when each record was made
Until AUSTRAC confirms they can be destroyed
cards.explanation: CDD records must be kept until the end of the 7-year period that begins when the business relationship ends, so to 1 May 2033. The 'from creation' rule applies to transaction records.

cards.title: A strong SMR narrative
cards.body:
In this fictional case, Tom's SMR on the structured cash deposits answered the questions an AUSTRAC analyst would ask:

- **Who:** the account holder, the four depositors identified on CCTV records and teller notes, and linked accounts.
- **What:** nine cash deposits totalling about AUD 86,000, each between AUD 9,000 and AUD 9,900.
- **When and where:** three days, four branches, with times.
- **Why suspicious:** amounts kept below the threshold, a depositor asking about the 'reporting limit', no business reason on file and immediate outward transfers.
- **What the bank did:** enhanced CDD started; account restricted under bank policy; no customer contact about the report.

A clear narrative turns a single alert into intelligence other agencies can use.

cards.title: Words to avoid at the counter
cards.body: Never say 'compliance is looking at you', 'we have to report this', 'it's for AUSTRAC', or 'keep it under 10k and it won't be reported'. The last one could help a customer avoid reporting and is a serious breach. Use ordinary, true service language, then escalate.

cards.title: Stage four take-aways
items: An SMR obligation arises around a designated service (provided, requested or asked about) plus a suspicion on reasonable grounds.
Deadline: 24 hours for suspected terrorism financing; 3 business days for most other suspicions.
Threshold transaction reports (physical currency of AUD 10,000 or more) and international value transfer reports are due within 10 business days.
Tipping off is a criminal offence where disclosure could prejudice an investigation, whether or not one has begun.
Keep transaction records 7 years from creation and CDD records 7 years after the relationship ends.

cards.prompt: Rehearse it: what exact words would you use if a customer asked you, face to face, whether the bank had reported them?

quiz.question: A person phones Banksia Harbour to ask whether it would open an account for his company. The call raises a strong suspicion that he is using a false identity. Can an SMR obligation arise even though no account was opened?
options: Yes; an inquiry about a service the bank ordinarily provides can be enough, together with the suspicion
No; suspicions about a false identity raised at the enquiry stage are reported to state police, not to AUSTRAC
Yes, but only if the person later becomes a customer
No; the obligation arises only once the bank provides a service
quiz.explanation: Section 41 covers people who inquire whether the bank would provide a designated service of a kind it ordinarily provides. A suspicion that the person is not who they claim to be is one of the listed grounds.

quiz.question: An analyst forms a suspicion of tax evasion on Monday. Under the Act, what is the latest the SMR may be lodged, assuming normal business days?
options: Tuesday, within 24 hours
The Monday of the following fortnight
The end of the calendar month
Thursday, 3 business days after the day the suspicion was formed
quiz.explanation: For suspicions other than terrorism financing, the deadline is 3 business days after the day the suspicion is formed. The 24-hour clock is for terrorism financing.

quiz.question: A customer deposits AUD 11,500 in cash from the sale of a boat, with a signed sale contract. Nothing else is unusual. What does the bank need to lodge?
options: A threshold transaction report within 10 business days
A suspicious matter report within 3 business days
Both a TTR and an SMR
No report, because the source is documented
quiz.explanation: A transfer of physical currency of AUD 10,000 or more is a threshold transaction, reported within 10 business days whether or not anything is suspicious. Without a suspicion, no SMR is needed.

quiz.question: A customer asks the teller: 'What's the most I can deposit in cash without the bank reporting it?' then deposits AUD 9,500. What is the best response from the bank?
options: Lodge a threshold transaction report for the AUD 9,500 deposit
Refuse the deposit and tell the customer why
Escalate internally so an SMR can be considered, without discussing reporting with the customer
Explain the AUD 10,000 threshold clearly so the customer understands how the reporting rules work
quiz.explanation: Asking how to avoid reporting is a structuring red flag. The teller should escalate without coaching the customer. A TTR does not apply below AUD 10,000, and explaining why the deposit is refused risks tipping off.

quiz.question: Which disclosure is most likely to be the tipping-off offence?
options: The compliance officer discusses the details of the SMR and the customer's history by phone with an AUSTRAC entrusted person
An investigator records the SMR reference number in the bank's case file
A teller tells a customer that a payment is going through standard checks
A relationship manager tells a client that 'compliance flagged your transfers to AUSTRAC, so be careful'
quiz.explanation: Revealing that a report was made to the subject could prejudice an investigation. Disclosure to AUSTRAC is outside the offence, internal case records are part of the bank's own process, and neutral service language reveals nothing.

quiz.question: A colleague argues that discussing an SMR with the customer is fine because 'no police investigation has started yet'. Why is this wrong?
options: Tipping off applies only once a court case is filed
The Act makes it irrelevant whether an investigation has commenced
Only AUSTRAC can decide when an investigation begins
Police investigations always start the day an SMR is lodged
quiz.explanation: Section 123 expressly provides that it does not matter whether an investigation has started; the question is whether disclosure would or could reasonably be expected to prejudice one.

quiz.question: Banksia Harbour receives an international transfer message from a bank in London for a customer's account in Sydney. What report does this usually trigger, and by when?
options: A threshold transaction report within 3 business days, because the money came from an overseas bank account
An SMR within 24 hours
An international value transfer report within 10 business days after receiving the transfer message
No report, because the money came into Australia
quiz.explanation: Section 46 requires a report about an international value transfer service within 10 business days after passing on or receiving the transfer message, in either direction. No suspicion is needed, so no SMR follows automatically.

quiz.question: Which record-keeping statement is correct under the amended Act?
options: Records may be kept in any language the bank chooses
Transaction records must be kept for 7 years from the day they are made
CDD records may be destroyed when the customer dies
Transaction records must be kept for 5 years after the account closes
quiz.explanation: Section 107 sets a 7-year period from the day a transaction record is made. CDD records run 7 years from the end of the relationship and must be in English or readily convertible into English.

quiz.question: An analyst suspects terrorism financing at 4 pm on a Friday before a long weekend. What does the Act require?
options: Lodge the SMR within 24 hours of forming the suspicion, even over the weekend
Lodge it by close of business on the next business day
Wait for the compliance officer to return and decide
Lodge it within 3 business days, so by Wednesday or Thursday after the long weekend
quiz.explanation: The terrorism financing deadline is 24 hours, counted in hours rather than business days, so banks need arrangements to report outside office hours.

quiz.question: Why does a well-written SMR narrative matter?
options: It allows the bank to close the customer's account without notice and without any further review
It turns the bank's observation into intelligence that AUSTRAC and partner agencies can act on
It replaces the need for enhanced CDD
It protects the customer's privacy from AUSTRAC
quiz.explanation: AUSTRAC analyses reports and shares them with partner agencies; a clear who-what-when-where-why narrative makes that possible. An SMR does not replace enhanced CDD where the relationship continues.

sessions.title: Sanctions, correspondent banking, people and readiness
sessions.summary: Handle sanctions matches under Australia's UN and autonomous sanctions laws, meet the correspondent banking and shell bank rules, apply personnel due diligence and training, and prepare for AUSTRAC scrutiny.
objectives: Handle a potential sanctions match and explain the reasonable precautions defence
Apply the shell bank prohibition and vostro due diligence and approval rules
Explain personnel due diligence and role-based training under the Act and Rules
Assemble evidence that the bank's AML/CTF program is working

cards.title: Stage five: the final watch
cards.setting: Institutional banking floor, Banksia Harbour Bank, Collins Street, Melbourne. 8:30 am.

lines.text: Final stage. Daniel Okafor, head of financial institutions banking, has two files on the table and a coffee going cold.
File one: Lagoon Pacific Bank wants a vostro account with us so it can clear AUD payments for its customers. Big opportunity.
File two: last night our screening stopped an outgoing payment. The beneficiary's name is a close match to a company on the DFAT Consolidated List.
Two classic final-stage problems: correspondent banking and sanctions. And both depend on people who know what they're doing.
Speaking of people: payments has three new contractors starting Monday. Has anyone checked them, or trained them?
Then that's stage five: sanctions, correspondent banking, personnel due diligence and training. Get this right and you're ready for the final exam.
