scenes.heading: Two sources
scenes.narration: Australia applies UN Security Council sanctions through the Charter of the United Nations Act 1945 and its own autonomous sanctions through the Autonomous Sanctions Act 2011.

scenes.heading: The Consolidated List
scenes.narration: The Australian Sanctions Office in DFAT keeps the Consolidated List of designated persons and entities, and administers permits and guidance.

scenes.heading: Don't deal, don't make available
scenes.narration: In broad terms, it is an offence to deal with the assets of a designated person or entity, or to make assets available to them, unless a permit allows it.

scenes.heading: Strict liability for companies
scenes.narration: For a body corporate, the autonomous sanctions offence is strict liability. The defence is to prove it took reasonable precautions and exercised due diligence to avoid the conduct.

scenes.heading: Linked to AML/CTF
scenes.narration: Since 31 March 2026, the AML/CTF Rules require a bank's AML/CTF policies to deal with targeted financial sanctions, and CDD must establish whether a customer or related person is designated.

cards.title: Handling a potential sanctions match
cards.caption: Your bank's sanctions procedure sets the detail; escalate to the sanctions team at the first hit.

items.label: Screen
items.detail: Customers, owners, agents and payment parties against the Consolidated List

items.label: Hold the payment or activity
items.detail: Do not process while the match is assessed

items.label: Investigate the match
items.detail: Compare identifiers: dates of birth, addresses, registration numbers

items.label: If true: freeze and do not make assets available
items.detail: No release without an ASO permit

items.label: Notify and report
items.detail: Contact the ASO as its guidance directs; consider an SMR to AUSTRAC

items.label: Record the decision
items.detail: Keep the evidence, reasoning and approvals

cards.question: What protects a company that breaches an autonomous sanction law despite its efforts?
options: Showing it did not know the person was designated
Proving it took reasonable precautions and exercised due diligence to avoid the conduct
Showing the amount involved was small
Reporting the breach to AUSTRAC within 3 business days
cards.explanation: The offence is strict liability for bodies corporate, so lack of knowledge is not a defence. The statutory defence is proving reasonable precautions and due diligence, which is why screening, procedures and staff training matter.

cards.title: Correspondent banking duties
cards.prompt: Match each obligation in Part 8 and Part 10 of the Act to what it requires.

pairs.right: Never enter a correspondent relationship with a shell bank or a bank that lets shell banks use its accounts
Assess a vostro respondent under the Rules and record it in writing
A senior officer approves before the vostro relationship begins
Within 20 business days, document each institution's responsibilities
Reassess the respondent at the times the Rules set, with written records
Keep the assessment records for 7 years after preparing them

cards.title: Personnel due diligence and training
cards.body:
The reforms put people inside the AML/CTF policies. Under **section 26F(4)(d) and (e)** of the Act and **sections 5-8 and 5-9** of the Rules, the policies must deal with:

- **Personnel due diligence:** checks on people who are, or will be, employed or engaged in roles relevant to the bank's AML/CTF obligations, including contractors.
- **Training:** for those people, **initial training** when they join and **ongoing training** during their employment or engagement.

The training must:
- suit the person's **function**, the **ML/TF/PF risks** of that function and their **responsibilities** under the policies;
- cover the bank's risks and its obligations under the Act, regulations and Rules;
- be **readily understandable**.

AUSTRAC expects banks to identify which roles need this, tailor it, refresh it as risks and laws change, and **keep completion records**. This quest is part of that training. It does not replace your bank's own policies.

cards.title: The contractors
cards.setting: Payments operations, Collins Street. Friday, 4:50 pm.

lines.text: The three payments contractors start Monday with full access to payment release. Procurement says vetting is 'the agency's job'.
We need them, Tom. Month-end volumes are brutal.
Releasing payments is an AML/CTF function. Our policies have to cover due diligence on contractors in those roles, not just employees.
And they need role-specific training before they release anything: red flags, sanctions holds and how to escalate.
Fine. Read-only access until the checks and training are done. I'll tell the agency.

cards.title: Lagoon Pacific Bank's vostro
cards.situation: Daniel's team wants to open Lagoon Pacific Bank's vostro account next week to win a mandate. The due diligence questionnaire came back incomplete: Lagoon will not say whether it provides accounts to other banks, and one of its own respondents is reportedly an unaffiliated bank with no physical presence in the country where it is licensed. No senior officer has signed off.

choices.text: Open the account now and finish due diligence in the first month; the mandate is valuable.
choices.outcome: Poor. The Act requires a due diligence assessment and senior officer approval before entering a vostro relationship, and prohibits relationships with institutions that let shell banks use their accounts.

choices.text: Pause: complete the due diligence assessment, resolve the shell bank question, and seek senior officer approval only if the risk is acceptable.
choices.outcome: Best. You meet the entry requirements in section 96 and address the section 95 shell bank prohibition before any relationship begins. If the answers stay unclear, the relationship should not proceed.

choices.text: Open the account but block payments until the questionnaire is complete.
choices.outcome: Partly right in limiting exposure, but opening the vostro account still enters the relationship before the required assessment and approval.

cards.title: Correspondent versus nested services
cards.caption: The Act defines a nested services relationship as one that is not correspondent banking.

items.label: What it is
items.left: Banking services from one financial institution to another, such as a vostro account
items.right: An overseas FI, remitter or VASP uses the bank's services to serve its own customers abroad

items.label: Key Act rules
items.left: Shell bank prohibition; due diligence and senior officer approval before vostro entry
items.right: Enhanced CDD is mandatory under section 32

items.label: Records
items.left: Assessment records kept for 7 years after preparation
items.right: CDD records kept for 7 years after the relationship ends

items.label: Typical owner
items.left: Financial institutions or correspondent banking team
items.right: Business banking, payments or FI teams

cards.title: Sanctions law, AML/CTF law, or both?
cards.prompt: Sort each duty by where it mainly comes from.

items.text: Do not make assets available to a designated person without a permit
Apply for a permit to deal with a frozen asset
Lodge an SMR within 3 business days of a suspicion
Report threshold cash transactions of AUD 10,000 or more
Train staff who screen and escalate sanctions matches
Establish during CDD whether a customer is designated for targeted financial sanctions
Keep evidence that the bank took reasonable precautions and due diligence

cards.title: Final exam recap: roles and numbers

cards.front: Who oversees the bank's ML/TF risk and compliance?
cards.back: The governing body (the board), as an ongoing duty under the Act.

cards.front: Who approves the risk assessment and policies?
cards.back: Senior managers designated in the AML/CTF policies.

cards.front: How often does the compliance officer report to the board?
cards.back: At least once every 12 months.

cards.front: Backstop for reviewing the risk assessment and policies?
cards.back: At least once every 3 years.
24 hours for suspected terrorism financing; 3 business days for most others.

cards.front: Who must approve a foreign PEP relationship?
cards.back: A senior manager, with enhanced CDD applied.

cards.front: Who approves a new vostro correspondent relationship?
cards.back: A senior officer, after a written due diligence assessment.
People in roles relevant to the AML/CTF obligations, including contractors: initial and ongoing, role-based.

cards.question: Which statement about AML/CTF training under the reformed Rules is correct?
options: One generic e-learning module a year for all staff is always enough
Training must be initial and ongoing, suited to each person's function and its risks, and readily understandable
Only the compliance team needs AML/CTF training
Training is optional if the staff member has passed personnel due diligence
cards.explanation: Rules section 5-9 requires initial and ongoing training suited to the person's function, its ML/TF/PF risks and their responsibilities, delivered in a readily understandable way. A single generic module may not meet that, and personnel due diligence does not replace training.

cards.title: Banksia Harbour's readiness check
cards.body:
Before AUSTRAC's next compliance assessment, Priya runs a fictional readiness check:

- **Risk assessment:** updated for Banksia Send; approved by the designated senior manager; next backstop review diarised.
- **Policies:** cover CDD, enhanced CDD, PEPs, reporting, targeted financial sanctions, correspondent banking, personnel due diligence and training.
- **Governance:** annual compliance officer report delivered to the board; minutes show challenge and follow-up.
- **Reporting:** SMR timeliness tracked, with a weekend roster for terrorism financing suspicions; TTR and transfer report errors reconciled.
- **Records:** retention rules tested by retrieving a closed customer's CDD file.
- **People:** contractor checks completed; role-based training records by team.

The gaps found (two overdue trainees, one unsigned correspondent review) go into a dated action plan.

cards.title: Stage five take-aways
items: Sanctions come from the Charter of the United Nations Act 1945 and the Autonomous Sanctions Act 2011, administered by the ASO in DFAT.
Companies face strict liability for autonomous sanctions breaches; the defence is reasonable precautions and due diligence.
Vostro correspondent relationships need a written due diligence assessment and senior officer approval before entry; shell banks are prohibited; records are kept 7 years.
AML/CTF policies must cover personnel due diligence and initial and ongoing, role-based, understandable training, with records kept.
A ready bank can show its risk assessment, policies, board reporting, reporting timeliness, records and training in evidence.

cards.prompt: If AUSTRAC asked you tomorrow to show how your role meets the bank's AML/CTF policies, what evidence could you produce, and what is missing?

quiz.question: A Banksia Harbour payment is stopped because the beneficiary closely matches an entity on the DFAT Consolidated List. What should happen first?
options: Return the funds to the sender with an explanation of the match
Keep the payment on hold and escalate so the match can be investigated against full identifiers
Release the payment and lodge an SMR afterwards
Release the payment as soon as the customer confirms in writing that the beneficiary is a different company
quiz.explanation: A potential match should be held and investigated before any processing. Releasing on the customer's word, or after the fact, risks making assets available to a designated person, and explaining the match could alert the parties.

quiz.question: Why are screening systems, written procedures and staff training so important to a bank's sanctions compliance in Australia?
options: They make the bank exempt from the Consolidated List
They transfer liability for breaches to individual staff
They are needed before the Australian Sanctions Office will issue or renew an Australian banking licence
They are the evidence a body corporate needs for the reasonable precautions and due diligence defence
quiz.explanation: The autonomous sanctions offence is strict liability for companies, with a defence for reasonable precautions and due diligence. Controls and training are how a bank proves that. Banking licences come from APRA.

quiz.question: Before entering a correspondent banking relationship involving a vostro account, what does the Act require?
options: Approval from AUSTRAC and the ASO
A signed questionnaire from the respondent only
A written due diligence assessment under the Rules and approval by a senior officer
Board approval of the respondent's AML/CTF policies
quiz.explanation: Section 96 requires the bank to carry out and record a due diligence assessment in line with the Rules, and a senior officer to approve, before entry. A questionnaire is an input to the assessment, not a substitute for it.

quiz.question: A prospective respondent bank lets an unaffiliated bank, licensed abroad but with no physical presence in its country of incorporation, use its accounts. What does the Act say?
options: The relationship is allowed if the shell bank is in a FATF member country
The relationship is allowed with senior officer approval
The bank must not enter into a correspondent relationship with that respondent
The relationship is allowed with enhanced CDD
quiz.explanation: Section 95 prohibits correspondent relationships with shell banks and with financial institutions that permit their accounts to be used by shell banks. No level of approval or extra diligence makes it permissible.

quiz.question: How long must a bank keep a correspondent banking due diligence assessment record?
options: 7 years after the record is prepared
5 years after the relationship ends
Until the next assessment replaces it
10 years from the start of the relationship
quiz.explanation: Section 117 requires correspondent banking records prepared under section 96 to be kept for 7 years after their preparation.

quiz.question: Three contractors will release payments at Banksia Harbour. Which approach fits the reformed AML/CTF Rules?
options: Give them the same generic module as head office staff at some point after their first month in the role
Rely on the agency's general checks and skip training for temporary staff
Exempt them because they are not employees
Apply personnel due diligence and give them role-based AML/CTF training before they perform the function
quiz.explanation: The policies must deal with due diligence and training for people employed or otherwise engaged in relevant roles, so contractors are covered. Training must suit their function and its risks.

quiz.question: Which feature is required of AML/CTF training under section 5-9 of the Rules?
options: It must be identical for every employee
It must be readily understandable by the people receiving it
It must be completed once, on joining
It must be delivered by AUSTRAC-accredited trainers
quiz.explanation: The Rules require training that suits the person's role and risks and is readily understandable, delivered both initially and on an ongoing basis. There is no AUSTRAC accreditation requirement, and identical training for all would not be tailored.

quiz.question: Which duty comes mainly from Australian sanctions laws rather than the AML/CTF Act?
options: Reporting physical currency transactions of AUD 10,000 or more
Not making assets available to a designated person without a permit
Reporting a suspicion to AUSTRAC within 3 business days
Keeping CDD records for 7 years after a relationship ends
quiz.explanation: The prohibition on dealing with or making assets available to designated persons comes from the sanctions laws administered by the ASO. The others are AML/CTF Act duties.

quiz.question: A financial institutions team says correspondent banking and nested services are 'the same thing'. Which reply is correct?
options: They are the same and both need only standard CDD
A nested services relationship excludes correspondent banking and triggers enhanced CDD
Nested services are banned in Australia
Correspondent banking is just one type of nested services relationship, so the same rules apply
quiz.explanation: The Act defines a nested services relationship as one that is not a correspondent banking relationship, and section 32 makes enhanced CDD mandatory for it. Correspondent banking has its own Part 8 rules.

quiz.question: Which piece of evidence would best show AUSTRAC that Banksia Harbour's governing body exercises ongoing oversight?
options: Board minutes showing the compliance officer's annual report was discussed, challenged and followed up
A list of SMRs lodged during the year
A signed copy of the approved AML/CTF policies, stored safely in the compliance team's shared network drive
An email from the CEO saying the bank takes AML/CTF seriously
quiz.explanation: Ongoing oversight is shown by the board receiving the compliance officer's report at least every 12 months and engaging with it. Policies, statements and SMR counts do not show the board's own oversight.

regulators: Australian Transaction Reports and Analysis Centre (AUSTRAC)
Australian Sanctions Office, Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade (ASO)

references.title: Anti-Money Laundering and Counter-Terrorism Financing Act 2006
references.issuer: Parliament of Australia (Federal Register of Legislation)
references.note: As amended by the 2024 reforms, the AML/CTF policies must deal with due diligence on people in AML/CTF-relevant roles and with training them on the entity's ML/TF/PF risks and legal obligations.

references.title: Anti-Money Laundering and Counter-Terrorism Financing Act 2006
references.issuer: Parliament of Australia (Federal Register of Legislation)
references.note: Risk assessment covering ML/TF/PF with review on triggers and at least every 3 years; no new service without a current assessment; policies reviewed at least every 3 years; governing body oversight; compliance officer notified to AUSTRAC within 14 days.

references.title: Anti-Money Laundering and Counter-Terrorism Financing Act 2006
references.issuer: Parliament of Australia (Federal Register of Legislation)
references.provision: Sections 28 and 30 (initial and ongoing CDD) and 32 (enhanced CDD triggers)
references.note: Initial CDD matters must be established on reasonable grounds before service starts; ongoing monitoring and risk review; enhanced CDD for high risk, continued service after an SMR, foreign PEPs, FATF high-risk jurisdictions and nested services.

references.title: Anti-Money Laundering and Counter-Terrorism Financing Act 2006
references.issuer: Parliament of Australia (Federal Register of Legislation)
references.provision: Sections 41(2) (SMR deadlines), 43 (threshold transactions), 46 (international value transfers) and 123 (tipping off)
references.note: SMRs within 24 hours for terrorism financing, otherwise 3 business days; physical currency of AUD 10,000 or more and international value transfers reported within 10 business days; disclosure that could prejudice an investigation is an offence.

references.title: Anti-Money Laundering and Counter-Terrorism Financing Act 2006
references.issuer: Parliament of Australia (Federal Register of Legislation)
references.note: No correspondent relationships involving shell banks; vostro due diligence and senior officer approval before entry; transaction records 7 years from creation, CDD records 7 years after the relationship ends, correspondent records 7 years.

references.title: Anti-Money Laundering and Counter-Terrorism Financing Amendment Act 2024
references.issuer: Parliament of Australia (Federal Register of Legislation)
references.note: Amending Act that restructured programs into a risk assessment plus AML/CTF policies, added proliferation financing and modernised CDD; most changes from 31 March 2026, tipping off from 31 March 2025, new sectors from 1 July 2026.

references.title: Anti-Money Laundering and Counter-Terrorism Financing Rules 2025
references.provision: Sections 5-3 (targeted financial sanctions), 5-5 (PEP approval), 5-7 (reports to governing body), 5-8 and 5-9 (personnel due diligence and training)
references.note: Policies must deal with targeted financial sanctions, require senior manager approval for foreign PEPs (and other PEPs where risk is high), provide compliance officer reports to the governing body at least every 12 months, and provide initial and ongoing role-based training.

references.title: Autonomous Sanctions Act 2011
references.issuer: Parliament of Australia (Federal Register of Legislation)
references.provision: Section 16(5)-(8) (body corporate offence, reasonable precautions defence)
references.note: A body corporate commits a strict liability offence if its conduct contravenes a sanction law, unless it proves it took reasonable precautions and exercised due diligence.

references.title: Suspicious matter reports
references.note: Explains SMR triggers and deadlines: 24 hours for suspected terrorism financing and 3 business days for other suspicions.

references.title: AML/CTF training
references.note: AUSTRAC expects training to cover the entity's obligations and risks, to be tailored by role, refreshed often enough to keep pace with risk and legal change, and recorded.

references.title: Governing body
references.note: The governing body must exercise ongoing oversight of ML/TF risk and compliance and receive compliance officer reports at least every 12 months.

references.title: Sanctions Compliance Toolkit
references.issuer: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade (Australian Sanctions Office)
references.note: ASO guidance listing ongoing staff training as a core element of a sanctions compliance program and as evidence of reasonable precautions and due diligence.

bank.question: In April 2026 a Banksia Harbour manager argues that, because the bank's last program review was in 2025, it can keep its Part A/Part B program until 2028. What is the best response?
options: The manager is right, unless AUSTRAC issues a remedial direction first
The manager is right, because existing programs continue unchanged until the next three-yearly review
Banks moved to the reformed obligations on 31 March 2026, so the new design already applies
The old program can continue until 1 July 2026, when the new sectors join
bank.explanation: Existing reporting entities such as banks moved to the reformed obligations on 31 March 2026. The three-year backstop governs reviews of a compliant program, not a transition period, and 1 July 2026 is the date for new sectors.

bank.question: Which statement correctly describes how AUSTRAC and the Australian Sanctions Office divide responsibilities?
options: The ASO supervises banks' CDD; AUSTRAC issues sanctions permits
Both bodies jointly approve each bank's AML/CTF policies
AUSTRAC maintains the Consolidated List, while the ASO receives suspicious matter and threshold reports from banks
AUSTRAC regulates AML/CTF and receives reports; the ASO administers sanctions and the Consolidated List
bank.explanation: AUSTRAC is the AML/CTF regulator and FIU, receiving SMRs and other reports. The ASO in DFAT administers UN and autonomous sanctions, keeps the Consolidated List and issues permits. Neither approves bank policies.

bank.question: Banksia Harbour's trade finance team has never considered whether its letters of credit could fund weapons programs. Which reformed requirement does this gap most directly breach?
options: Letters of credit automatically require enhanced CDD
The governing body must personally approve every trade finance transaction above a set limit
Trade finance must be reported as threshold transactions
The ML/TF risk assessment must identify and assess proliferation financing risk
bank.explanation: Since the reforms, the risk assessment must cover proliferation financing as well as ML and TF, so a trade finance PF blind spot is a gap. The other options describe obligations that do not exist.

bank.question: AUSTRAC considers that a bank's breaches are serious and systemic, and that the bank's remediation has been slow. Which outcome can only be imposed by a court?
options: A civil penalty order requiring the bank to pay a pecuniary penalty
A remedial direction to fix the contravention
Acceptance of an enforceable undertaking
A requirement to appoint an external auditor
bank.explanation: Pecuniary penalties for civil penalty provisions are ordered by the Federal Court on AUSTRAC's application. Remedial directions, enforceable undertakings and external audits are tools AUSTRAC uses without first going to court.

bank.question: Which change is NOT part of the 2024 reforms as they apply to banks?
options: A requirement that AUSTRAC approve each bank's AML/CTF policies before use
Framing initial CDD as a set of matters to be established on reasonable grounds
Giving the governing body an explicit oversight duty
Adding proliferation financing to the risk assessment
bank.explanation: The reforms added PF, outcome-based CDD and an explicit governing body duty. AUSTRAC does not pre-approve policies; designated senior managers in the bank approve them.

bank.question: A new employee asks why the AML/CTF Act applies to her role in a branch that only sells home loans. What is the most accurate answer?
options: The Act applies to her only if she lodges SMRs
The Act applies only to the specific roles that are named in APRA's prudential standards for authorised banks
Making loans is a designated service, so the obligations attach to the services she helps provide
The Act applies only to staff who handle cash
bank.explanation: The Act's obligations attach to designated services, which include lending. Staff involved in providing those services are covered by the bank's AML/CTF policies, whether or not they handle cash.

bank.question: Which lesson from the Commonwealth Bank (2018) and Westpac (2020) civil penalty cases is most relevant to the reformed governing body duty?
options: Boards should delegate AML/CTF entirely to the compliance officer and simply note the annual report
Oversight matters only after AUSTRAC starts court proceedings
Directors must oversee whether AML/CTF systems actually work, not just whether policies exist
Directors are personally liable for every late report
bank.explanation: Both cases involved systems that failed at scale, raising questions about oversight. The reformed Act now requires the governing body to exercise ongoing oversight and take reasonable steps, which cannot be fully delegated.

bank.question: On which date did newly regulated professions, such as many lawyers and real estate agents, become subject to the reformed AML/CTF obligations?
options: 31 March 2026
31 March 2025
1 July 2026
10 December 2024
bank.explanation: Tranche two sectors joined on 1 July 2026. 31 March 2026 was the date for existing reporting entities like banks, and 31 March 2025 the start of the new tipping-off offence.

bank.question: Banksia Harbour's risk assessment was last reviewed in May 2024. No significant change has occurred and AUSTRAC has sent no relevant information. By when, at the latest, must the next review happen?
options: Only when a significant change occurs
By May 2025, under an annual cycle
By May 2031, aligned with record retention
By May 2027, under the three-year backstop
bank.explanation: The Act requires review on triggers and in any event at least once every three years. With no trigger, the backstop is three years from the last review.

bank.question: The board risk committee wants to sign off the ML/TF risk assessment itself instead of a senior manager. What does the reformed Act require?
options: The compliance officer must approve it alone
The policies must designate senior managers to approve the assessment and policies
Only the governing body may approve the risk assessment, because it carries ultimate accountability
No approval is needed if AUSTRAC has reviewed it
bank.explanation: Section 26F(4)(c) requires the policies to designate senior managers responsible for approving the risk assessment and policies. The governing body's statutory role is oversight, although it may of course review them.

bank.question: Banksia Harbour's compliance officer reports to a mid-level operations manager, has no budget and needs business approval to contact AUSTRAC. Which requirement is most clearly not met?
options: The compliance officer must be a board member
The compliance officer must hold a law degree
The compliance officer must be approved by APRA under the fit and proper standard before starting in the role
The compliance officer must be at management level with sufficient authority, independence and resources
bank.explanation: The Act requires a management-level compliance officer with sufficient authority, independence and resources, whose functions include communicating with AUSTRAC. There are no board-membership, degree or APRA-approval requirements.

bank.question: Which pair of duties belongs to the governing body under section 26H?
options: Notifying AUSTRAC of the compliance officer and keeping records
Approving the risk assessment and lodging SMRs
Designating senior managers and verifying customers
Ongoing oversight of risk and compliance, and taking reasonable steps to ensure risks are managed
bank.explanation: Section 26H requires the governing body to exercise appropriate ongoing oversight and take reasonable steps to ensure the bank manages its risks and complies. Approval sits with senior managers, and notifications and records are entity duties.

bank.question: Banksia Harbour appoints a new compliance officer on 1 September. On 25 September nobody has told AUSTRAC. What is the position?
options: Notification is required only at the annual compliance report
No notification is needed, because the previous compliance officer was already notified to AUSTRAC
The bank has 30 days, so it is still on time
The bank is late: AUSTRAC must be notified within 14 days of the designation
bank.explanation: Section 26M requires notification of the designated compliance officer within 14 days. By 25 September that period has passed.

bank.question: Banksia Harbour acquires a small fintech that offers instant cross-border payments to Asia and plans to offer the service to bank customers next month. Which step must come before the launch?
options: Lodge a threshold transaction report for the acquisition price paid for the fintech business
Update the risk assessment for the new service, channel and countries before launch
Have the governing body approve each new customer
Notify APRA and wait for its approval
bank.explanation: A bank must not start providing a designated service without an up-to-date risk assessment, and new services, channels and countries are significant changes. APRA approval and TTRs are not the relevant requirement.

bank.question: Which statement about the AML/CTF policies is correct under section 26F?
options: They may cover CDD procedures only, because reporting obligations are handled by AUSTRAC itself directly
They must follow an AUSTRAC template and be re-approved every year
Manage assessed risks, ensure compliance, suit the business and be reviewed at least every 3 years
They apply only to staff who deal with customers face to face
bank.explanation: Section 26F requires policies that manage the risks, ensure compliance, are proportionate, and are reviewed at least every three years. There is no mandatory template or annual re-approval, and reporting duties sit with the bank.

bank.question: The compliance officer's annual report shows recurring late international transfer reports. The board notes the report without discussion. Which risk does this create?
options: The report must be lodged with AUSTRAC as an SMR
The bank must re-do its risk assessment within 24 hours
The compliance officer becomes personally liable for the late reports
The governing body may not be exercising the appropriate ongoing oversight the Act requires
bank.explanation: Ongoing oversight means engaging with reported problems and taking reasonable steps to ensure they are fixed. Merely noting a report of recurring breaches risks falling short of the section 26H duty.

bank.question: AUSTRAC sends banks a typology alert about criminals using business accounts to move scam proceeds through payment apps. Banksia Harbour offers both. What is the right response?
options: Treat it as a trigger to review the risk assessment and adjust policies and monitoring where needed
File the alert and consider it at the next three-yearly review
Ask AUSTRAC to confirm in writing whether the bank is actually affected before taking any action at all
Lodge SMRs on all business customers using payment apps
bank.explanation: AUSTRAC communicating risk information relevant to the bank's services is a statutory review trigger. Blanket SMRs without suspicion are inappropriate, and the bank must act rather than wait.

bank.question: A customer applies for a business account for a family trust. The trustee is verified, but the bank has not worked out who controls the trust or why it needs the account. What should happen?
options: Hold off until the beneficial owners and purpose are established on reasonable grounds
Open the account with a lower transaction limit
Open the account now, because the trustee has already been fully verified with photo ID
Open the account and lodge an SMR to be safe
bank.explanation: Initial CDD requires the beneficial owners and the nature and purpose of the relationship to be established on reasonable grounds before service starts. Limits or an SMR do not cure missing CDD.

bank.question: During onboarding, a customer's authorised signatory turns out to be a person designated on the DFAT Consolidated List. Which CDD matter has the bank just established?
options: That a threshold transaction has occurred
That a person acting on behalf of the customer is designated for targeted financial sanctions
That the customer is a domestic politically exposed person
That the customer's ML/TF risk is low
bank.explanation: Initial CDD must establish whether anyone acting on behalf of the customer is a person designated for targeted financial sanctions. This finding requires immediate escalation under the sanctions procedure.

bank.question: Which customer does NOT trigger mandatory enhanced CDD under section 32, as long as the bank's risk rating is not high?
options: A foreign remitter using the bank's account to serve its customers abroad
An Australian state government minister holding a personal savings account
An individual physically present in a jurisdiction on FATF's call-for-action list
A company whose beneficial owner is a deputy minister of a foreign country
bank.explanation: A domestic PEP needs enhanced CDD only where the risk is high. Foreign PEPs, people in FATF call-for-action jurisdictions and nested services relationships are automatic section 32 triggers.

bank.question: Under the Rules, who must approve before Banksia Harbour begins serving a foreign PEP?
options: A senior manager
AUSTRAC
The customer's relationship manager
The governing body
bank.explanation: The Rules require the policies to provide for senior manager approval before serving foreign PEPs. The board's role is oversight, and relationship managers are not the approvers.

bank.question: A low-risk customer of eight years starts receiving large payments from a newly formed offshore company and immediately wires them to third parties. The relationship manager says the customer is 'known to us'. What does the Act expect?
options: Rely on the long history and take no action until the scheduled review
Close the account immediately and tell the customer why
Ask the customer to sign a statutory declaration that all the funds are legitimate and then continue as normal, given the history
Monitor and act on the unusual behaviour: review and update the risk rating, refresh KYC and consider whether an SMR is due
bank.explanation: Ongoing CDD requires monitoring for unusual transactions and reviewing the customer's risk when they appear. History does not freeze the rating, a declaration is not verification, and explaining a closure could tip off.

bank.question: Banksia Harbour verifies a high-risk customer's identity using only a utility bill and a letter the customer's company prepared. What is the main weakness?
options: Utility bills may never be used for any verification
Higher-risk customers need verification using reliable, independent data, in proportion to risk
The bank should have checked the customer's social media profile and company website instead of documents
Verification is not required for corporate customers
bank.explanation: The Act requires verification of KYC information using reliable and independent data appropriate to the customer's risk. A self-prepared letter is not independent, and a high-risk customer needs stronger verification.

bank.question: Banksia Harbour decides to continue serving a customer after lodging an SMR about him. A colleague says nothing changes because 'the report is AUSTRAC's problem now'. Why is this wrong?
options: Continuing service after an SMR obligation arises makes enhanced CDD mandatory under section 32
The bank must close every account that is the subject of an SMR
The bank must tell the customer that monitoring has increased
AUSTRAC must approve any continued service after an SMR
bank.explanation: Section 32 makes enhanced CDD mandatory where an SMR obligation has arisen and the bank proposes to keep providing services. There is no automatic closure or AUSTRAC approval, and telling the customer risks tipping off.

bank.question: A customer is the head of a UN agency's regional office and is rated high risk because of large unexplained transfers. What applies?
options: Enhanced CDD only if she is also a foreign national
Standard CDD, because international organisation PEPs are always low risk
Enhanced CDD and senior manager approval, because she is an international organisation PEP and the risk is high
Refusal, because international organisation PEPs are not permitted to hold personal accounts with Australian banks
bank.explanation: International organisation PEPs need enhanced CDD and senior manager approval where the risk is high, and the high rating is also a section 32 trigger in its own right. Nationality is not the test.

bank.question: Which situation best illustrates the 'reasonable grounds' standard in initial CDD?
options: The customer has signed a statement that all information is true
The bank holds objective, verified information that supports its conclusion about each required matter
A senior staff member feels comfortable with the customer after a long face-to-face meeting at the branch
The customer has banked with another Australian bank for years
bank.explanation: Reasonable grounds means an objective basis supported by information the bank has collected and verified in proportion to risk. Self-declarations, gut feeling or another bank's relationship are not enough on their own.

bank.question: A customer withdraws AUD 9,800 in cash on Monday and AUD 9,700 on Tuesday, refusing to say what it is for and asking whether 'under ten' avoids paperwork. What should the bank consider?
options: Two threshold transaction reports, one for each withdrawal
An SMR, as the pattern and question suggest structuring though neither withdrawal hits the threshold
No report, because neither withdrawal reaches AUD 10,000
A single threshold transaction report for the combined AUD 19,500, lodged within 10 business days of Tuesday
bank.explanation: Each withdrawal is below AUD 10,000, so the TTR rules are not met, but splitting cash and asking how to avoid reporting is a classic structuring red flag that can found a suspicion and an SMR.

bank.question: An analyst forms a suspicion on Thursday that a customer is laundering drug proceeds. Assuming Friday, Monday and Tuesday are business days, when is the SMR due at the latest?
options: By the second Thursday after
By the end of Monday
By the end of Tuesday
By Friday at the same time
bank.explanation: For non-terrorism suspicions the deadline is 3 business days after the day the suspicion is formed: Friday, Monday and Tuesday. Twenty-four hours applies only to terrorism financing.

bank.question: Which situation can give rise to the 24-hour SMR deadline?
options: A suspicion that funds may relate to financing terrorism
A suspicion that a customer is evading tax
A suspicion that a customer is using a false name
Any transaction over AUD 10,000 in cash
bank.explanation: Section 41 sets 24 hours where the suspicion relates to terrorism financing. Tax evasion and identity suspicions follow the 3 business day deadline, and cash over the threshold is a TTR matter.

bank.question: Two weeks after an SMR, the customer's accountant calls Banksia Harbour's relationship manager to ask whether 'anything has been sent to AUSTRAC'. What should the relationship manager do?
options: Confirm the report, because the customer's accountant is bound by strict professional confidentiality rules
Give no information about any report, use neutral service language and tell compliance about the call
Deny any report exists, to protect the investigation
Explain that the law prevents discussion of reports to AUSTRAC
bank.explanation: Disclosing that an SMR was made could prejudice an investigation, whoever asks. A false denial is not needed, and mentioning the legal prohibition signals that a report exists. The call itself is useful information for compliance.

bank.question: Which statement about the tipping-off offence in section 123 is correct?
options: It applies only to disclosures made after a police investigation formally opens
It applies only to the compliance officer who lodged the report
It covers SMR information where disclosure could prejudice an investigation
It was introduced on 31 March 2026 with the other reforms
bank.explanation: The offence covers disclosures of SMR-related information that would or could reasonably be expected to prejudice an investigation, whether or not one has commenced. It covers officers, employees and agents, and started on 31 March 2025.

bank.question: Banksia Harbour sends a customer's payment from Brisbane to a supplier in Japan. Separately, it has no suspicion about the customer. Which report is due?
options: A threshold transaction report within 10 business days, because the payment is well over AUD 10,000
No report, because the customer is low risk
An international value transfer report within 10 business days of passing on the transfer message
A suspicious matter report within 3 business days
bank.explanation: International transfers through the bank's Australian operations trigger a report under section 46 within 10 business days, regardless of suspicion or customer risk. TTRs relate to physical currency.

bank.question: A customer relationship ended on 30 June 2026. A transaction record for that customer was made on 15 March 2020. Which retention dates apply?
options: The CDD records until 30 June 2033; the 2020 transaction record until 15 March 2027
Both records until 30 June 2033
Both records until 15 March 2027
The CDD records until 30 June 2031; the transaction record until 30 June 2033
bank.explanation: CDD records are kept for 7 years after the relationship ends (to 30 June 2033), while transaction records are kept for 7 years from the day they were made (to 15 March 2027).

bank.question: A teller, trying to be helpful, tells a cash customer that 'deposits under AUD 10,000 don't get reported'. Why is this a serious problem?
options: It is fine because the threshold is public information
It is a problem only because the threshold is actually AUD 5,000
It can help the customer avoid reporting, and smaller deposits in a suspicious pattern may still be reported
It is a problem only if the customer later deposits more than AUD 10,000 in a single transaction at any branch
bank.explanation: Coaching customers around the threshold can facilitate structuring, and smaller deposits can still lead to an SMR when they form a suspicious pattern. The threshold for physical currency is AUD 10,000.

bank.question: Screening confirms that a corporate customer is owned by a person newly designated on the DFAT Consolidated List. The customer asks to withdraw its balance today. What is the correct approach?
options: Close the account and send the balance to the customer by cheque
Do not release; freeze and escalate, as dealing with the assets needs an ASO permit
Release the funds and lodge an SMR afterwards
Release the funds, because the customer company itself is not named on the Consolidated List
bank.explanation: Assets owned or controlled by a designated person are generally caught, so releasing or paying out the balance risks dealing with them or making them available. Any dealing needs an ASO permit. Paying by cheque is still a release.

bank.question: Banksia Harbour breaches an autonomous sanctions law because a payment slipped past screening. Which fact would most help its defence?
options: Evidence that it lodged an SMR within 24 hours
Evidence that no employee at any level knew the beneficiary had been designated at the time the payment was sent
Evidence that the payment was below AUD 10,000
Evidence that it had reasonable precautions in place, such as tested screening, procedures and trained staff
bank.explanation: For a body corporate the offence is strict liability, so lack of knowledge is not a defence; proving reasonable precautions and due diligence is. The payment's size and SMR timing do not establish that defence.

bank.question: Banksia Harbour entered a vostro relationship on 1 March. On 10 April it still has no document setting out each institution's responsibilities. What is the problem?
options: The written record of responsibilities was due within 20 business days of entering the relationship
Nothing, because the responsibilities record is due only at the time of the first ongoing assessment
The record must be lodged with AUSTRAC, not kept by the bank
The record is needed only for nostro relationships
bank.explanation: Section 96 requires a written record of both institutions' responsibilities within 20 business days after entering a vostro relationship. By 10 April that period has passed.

bank.question: A senior officer approved a correspondent relationship before any due diligence assessment was prepared, saying 'the respondent is a well-known bank'. What is wrong?
options: A written due diligence assessment must come before entry and before approval
Well-known banks are exempt from correspondent due diligence
The governing body, not a senior officer, must approve
Nothing, because a senior officer's approval is the only requirement the Act imposes for entry
bank.explanation: Section 96 requires both a due diligence assessment carried out under the Rules with a written record and senior officer approval before entry. Reputation does not replace the assessment.

bank.question: Which group most clearly needs personnel due diligence and role-based training under section 26F(4) and Rules ss 5-8 and 5-9?
options: Only board directors and senior managers
Staff and contractors in roles relevant to AML/CTF obligations, such as payment release
Only permanent employees who work in the compliance department, including the compliance officer
Only staff who have previously breached a policy
bank.explanation: The policies must cover due diligence and training for people employed or otherwise engaged in functions relevant to the AML/CTF obligations, which includes contractors in roles like payment release.

bank.question: Banksia Harbour gives all 4,000 staff the same 20-minute module every two years, and nobody records completion. Which two weaknesses stand out against the Rules and AUSTRAC's expectations?
options: The module should be in a language other than English
The training is not tailored to each role's function and risks, and completion is not recorded
The module is too short and should be delivered by AUSTRAC
Staff should be trained only on joining, not every two years
bank.explanation: The Rules require training suited to each person's function, its risks and their responsibilities, and AUSTRAC expects completion records. AUSTRAC does not deliver bank training, and ongoing training is required.

bank.question: Which piece of evidence would best support Banksia Harbour's claim that its CDD records meet the Act?
options: A list of all accounts opened in the last year
A short policy statement saying that all customer records are kept 'for as long as needed' by the business
A screenshot of the customer's latest transaction
A closed customer's CDD file retrieved in English, within the 7-year period after the relationship ended
bank.explanation: Testing retrieval of a closed customer's CDD file shows records are kept for the required period after the relationship ends and are in English or readily convertible. A vague policy or account list proves neither.

bank.question: AUSTRAC asks Banksia Harbour to demonstrate its AML/CTF program. Which set of documents best covers the core of the reformed regime?
options: The risk assessment, approved policies, board reports, reporting data, records and training evidence
The Banking Code of Practice and the complaints register
The bank's annual report, capital management plan, credit policies and the latest external audit opinion
A list of SMRs lodged and the names of reported customers
bank.explanation: The reformed regime centres on the risk assessment, policies, governance, reporting, records and personnel due diligence and training. Capital, credit and complaints documents belong to other regimes.
